LightShed Says Paramount Must Sell Off Part of Warner Before March or Lose the Deal and $7 Billion
Trial runs March 2 to 19, 2027, briefs are due April 5, and the merger agreement dies June 4 with a $7 billion break fee. Paramount had asked for a November trial.
CEO Summary
LightShed Partners argued this morning that Paramount Skydance must settle the state antitrust suits before trial or lose Warner Bros. Discovery outright, because the calendar no longer allows an appeal. Trial is set for March 2 to 19, 2027, post-trial briefs are due April 5, and the merger agreement expires June 4, 2027, at which point Paramount owes a $7 billion break fee that the Ellison family would fund by buying equity at $16 per share. Paramount stock traded at $9.12 Thursday morning. LightShed's proposed remedies include selling one of the two studio lots along with franchise IP such as Harry Potter, DC and Dune, or shedding the Turner networks including TBS, TNT and CNN.
Why This Matters
The gap between the end of trial and the outside date is the operative number here. Post-trial briefs are due April 5, 2027, and the merger agreement lapses June 4. That leaves roughly eight weeks for Paramount to negotiate, document and execute any structural remedy before the deal dies automatically and the $7 billion break fee triggers. That compression hands settlement leverage to the plaintiff attorneys general, who can extract concessions simply by running the litigation to its scheduled conclusion rather than negotiating a resolution before trial.
Specific Implication
A production, rights arrangement, or executive relationship tied to Harry Potter, DC, Dune, or a Turner network sits inside a divestiture scenario keyed to the March 2027 trial date and the June 4, 2027 outside date. That exposure applies independent of whether the merger ultimately closes.
The Facts
  • Trial: March 2 to 19, 2027, before Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin. Post-trial briefs due April 5, 2027. Paramount had proposed November 2026.
  • Merger agreement expiration: June 4, 2027. Break fee: $7 billion.
  • Break fee funding per LightShed: Ellison family contributes $7 billion cash to Paramount for equity at $16 per share. PSKY traded at $9.12 on Thursday morning.
  • Plaintiffs: 12 state attorneys general plus the Writers Guild of America. California AG Rob Bonta has signaled he wants the deal blocked rather than settled.
  • Studio remedy floated: sell one of the two lots, its theatrical distribution infrastructure, franchise IP including Harry Potter, DC Comics and Dune, plus a share of the library.
  • Networks remedy floated: shed the Turner networks (TBS, TNT, CNN), leaving Paramount acquiring only Discovery Global Networks out of roughly 50 cable networks.
  • Comparable cited: Disney sold its 50% of A&E Networks to Hearst at under 3.5x EV/EBITDA.
  • If the deal terminates, LightShed expects WBD to split into Warner Bros. studio/HBO and Discovery Global Networks, and names Netflix and a post-split NBCUniversal as possible buyers.

The FCC Repealed the Broadcast Ownership Cap on a 2-1 Vote and Its Own Democrat Called It Unlawful
Anna Gomez cited three Republicans, including the former House Majority Leader who negotiated the 39 percent cap, saying only Congress can change it. Sinclair's CEO says he will transact as soon as the order hits the Federal Register.
CEO Summary
The FCC voted 2-1 along party lines Thursday to eliminate the 39% national cap on the share of U.S. television households a single station owner may reach. Chairman Brendan Carr argued broadcasters are constrained by anachronistic rules while Google, Netflix, Meta and Amazon reach the world unimpeded. Commissioner Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat, called the move "unlawful on its face" because Congress set the cap in 2012, citing agreement from former FCC Commissioner Mike O'Rielly, former House Majority Leader Tom DeLay and Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz. Two station-group deals sit behind the change: Nexstar-Tegna, which would reach 80% of U.S. households and is already enjoined by eight state attorneys general, and a revived Sinclair-Scripps.
Why This Matters
Ripley's "transact shortly after" timeline treats Federal Register publication as the gating event, but the Nexstar-Tegna precedent shows integration can be frozen by a state-attorney-general suit filed after a deal signs, not before it. The same eight-AG coalition that enjoined Nexstar-Tegna in April 2026 remains available to challenge Sinclair-Scripps on identical grounds. That makes the real closing risk on any repeal-enabled deal a post-signing state court action rather than the FCC's own vote count.
The Facts
  • Vote was 2-1: Carr and Republican commissioner Olivia Trusty for repeal; Gomez against.
  • The cap removed is 39% of reach among U.S. TV households, set by Congress in 2012. Its origins are in 1940s radio ownership regulation.
  • Gomez: "The FCC's decision to eliminate the 39% national audience reach cap is unlawful on its face. Congress set this cap in federal law, and only Congress can change it."
  • Gomez cited O'Rielly ("unequivocal that the FCC lacks authority"), DeLay (Congress wrote the cap to keep the FCC from changing it) and Cruz (skeptical a change can be made absent an act of Congress).
  • Carr: "Repealing the national cap will provide essential relief for local broadcasters by restoring a healthy counterbalance to the growing leverage of national programmers."
  • Nexstar-Tegna would reach 80% of U.S. television households. A court enjoined merger integration in April 2026 in a suit by eight state attorneys general; trial is set for July 6, 2027. Nexstar's Ninth Circuit appeal seeking to narrow the injunction is expected to be argued in Q4 2026.
  • Sinclair CEO Chris Ripley, August 5 earnings call: "we fully expect people to challenge this order," but the FCC is "on solid legal ground," and Sinclair will "be able to transact under this new rule shortly after the vote happens as soon as it gets into the federal registry."
  • Sinclair made an unsolicited offer for Scripps in fall 2025; the Scripps board rejected it in December. Sinclair operates or services 185 stations in 85 markets; Scripps has 60-plus stations in 40-plus markets.
  • NAB president and CEO Curtis LeGeyt called it "a generational step toward strengthening local stations."
  • Nexstar chief communications officer Gary Weitman called the decision "welcome, necessary and long-overdue."

Warner Bros. Discovery Studio Earnings Fell 89 Percent and Supergirl Is the Worst DC Release Since Catwoman
One year without the NBA took 22 percent of WBD's advertising revenue, $1.7 billion for the quarter, while streaming EBITDA rose 75 percent to $512 million.
CEO Summary
Warner Bros. Discovery reported Q2 revenue down 11% to $8.7 billion against $9.2 billion expected, with diluted EPS of 6 cents beating an expected 10-cent loss. The studio division fell hardest: revenue down 39% to $2.3 billion and adjusted EBITDA down 89% to $96 million, with Supergirl grossing $126 million worldwide, the lowest for any DC release since Catwoman in 2004. Streaming went the other way, revenue up 10% to $3.1 billion and EBITDA up 75% to $512 million, while total advertising fell 22% to $1.7 billion on the absence of the NBA.
Why This Matters
A studio segment whose adjusted EBITDA can fall 89% on the underperformance of one release has no slate depth to absorb a single miss, which is the vulnerability Zaslav's "no DC strategy shift" comment does not address. Streaming's 75% EBITDA growth in the same quarter means the company can currently paper over a theatrical shortfall in the consolidated numbers. That offset depends on streaming outperformance continuing at a pace the studio division cannot itself generate.
The Facts
  • Total revenue: $8.7 billion, down 11%. Analyst consensus: $9.2 billion. Diluted EPS: 6 cents, versus an expected loss of 10 cents.
  • Studio: revenue $2.3 billion, down 39%. Adjusted EBITDA $96 million, down 89%.
  • Supergirl: $126 million worldwide, lowest DC release since Catwoman (2004).
  • Streaming: revenue $3.1 billion, up 10%. EBITDA $512 million, up 75%.
  • Total advertising: $1.7 billion, down 22%.
  • Global Linear Networks: revenue $3.99 billion, down 17%. Adjusted EBITDA $1.4 billion, down 4%.
  • TheWrap reported quarterly profit down 91%.
  • Context: the $110 billion Paramount merger is in legal limbo, with 12 state attorneys general and the WGA suing to block and trial set for March 2027.
  • David Zaslav said Thursday the Superman sequel looks "amazing," that there is no DC strategy shift after Supergirl, and that staff are "working extremely hard" through the merger uncertainty.

Fox Refuses to Reopen Its NFL Contract and Tells the League Nothing Changes Until 2030
The NFL wrote an opt-out into all its 11-year pacts so it could reprice mid-term. Lachlan Murdoch told investors Fox "will not be making any amendments" before 2030.
CEO Summary
Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch told investors Thursday that Fox will not amend its current NFL rights deal, which runs through the 2029 season, despite the league seeking to invoke an opt-out clause written into the 11-year contracts it signed with all of its media partners to reset terms to market. The NFL has been holding the same conversation with Amazon, Disney, NBCUniversal and CBS. Murdoch said the relationship remains "incredibly positive" and that Fox sees "a clear path forward" after 2029.
Why This Matters
NBC reportedly paying more for its current NBA rights than for Sunday Night Football sets the comparison the NFL will use in every other reopener it pursues. Any partner who eventually renegotiates is pricing against basketball's newer, richer deal rather than against the NFL's own prior terms. That pushes the floor for a mid-term reset above where Fox's untouched 2029 contract currently sits.
Specific Implication
Fox's refusal sets no binding precedent for the NFL's separate talks with Amazon, Disney, NBCUniversal and CBS, since each holds different opt-out timing and contract terms.
The Facts
  • Fox's NFL deal runs through the end of the 2029 season. Murdoch: "We don't see any changes" until 2030; the company "will not be making any amendments."
  • The opt-out clause sits in the 11-year pacts the NFL struck with all of its media partners, allowing terms to be updated to market levels.
  • The league is also in discussions with Amazon, Disney, NBCUniversal and CBS.
  • NBC is believed to be paying more for its current NBA rights than for Sunday Night Football.
  • The NFL has held what are believed to be serious talks with Paramount Skydance about the CBS Sunday-afternoon package; the Redstone-to-Ellison change of control gave the league the right to reopen.
  • The NFL cannot exercise an opt-out on Disney's Monday Night Football deal until after 2030. A recent transaction made the NFL a minority owner of ESPN in exchange for control of NFL Network and other league media assets.
  • Disney announced Wednesday it had sold out all commercial inventory for its 2027 Super Bowl LXI broadcast, months earlier than networks typically disclose.
  • Murdoch praised a recent transaction giving Fox rights to NFL games via its Mexican properties.
  • The NFL, CBS Sports, NBC Sports and Prime Video sports did not comment.

YouTube Is Taking Peacock's Library as Brand-Safety Insurance Against Its Own AI Slop
A new YouTube account was served 500 Shorts and 21 percent were pure AI slop. Peacock's NFL games, Bravo originals and Law & Order now sit inside YouTube Premium at no extra charge.
CEO Summary
NBCUniversal has placed all ad-supported Peacock Premium content, including NFL games, Bravo originals and Law & Order, inside YouTube Premium at no additional charge for now, with terms undisclosed. Peacock has roughly 48 million subscribers against an estimated 125 million for YouTube Premium worldwide, but Antenna measured Peacock churn at 7% in June, three points above the weighted average. Wolfe Research's Peter Supino called the deal a possible step toward NBCUniversal exiting retail streaming, while Puck argues YouTube's motive is advertiser confidence ahead of a generative-AI content surge.
Why This Matters
Peacock still carries part of NBCUniversal's $2.5 billion annual NBA deal even after turning profitable last quarter. It accepted a placement deal with no incremental subscriber charge despite YouTube Premium's audience already running more than 2.5 times Peacock's own. That supports Supino's read that NBCUniversal priced this for cost relief rather than reach: a service losing subscribers at 7% monthly churn gains more from shedding distribution cost than from adding viewers on a platform where it already trails.
Specific Implication
A studio or rights holder licensing finished, professionally produced library content into a platform carrying significant AI-generated volume has a brand-safety rationale, distinct from audience reach, to raise in that negotiation.
The Facts
  • Deal: all ad-supported Peacock Premium content, including NFL games, Bravo originals and Law & Order, placed on YouTube Premium at no extra charge for now. Financial terms undisclosed.
  • Scale: Peacock about 48 million subscribers. YouTube Premium estimated at 125 million worldwide including YouTube Music, with 10 to 20 million in the U.S.
  • Churn: Antenna estimates Peacock at 7% in June, about three points above the weighted average.
  • Cost base: Peacock carries part of NBCU's $2.5 billion annual NBA deal. It converted to profitability last quarter.
  • Ad-free subscribers still pay for Peacock Premium Plus.
  • Wolfe Research's Peter Supino: the deal "could be a step towards NBCUniversal exiting the retail streaming business in order to shed costs," with a risk that some customers cancel more lucrative YouTube TV subscriptions.
  • Google chief business officer Philipp Schindler: YouTube's subscription business "is growing faster than ads, particularly driven by YouTube Music and Premium."
  • YouTube AI policy: VP of trust and safety Matt Halprin last month named three non-monetizable categories, generic or repetitive content, "unsatisfying" content, and AI personas discussing sensitive topics.
  • Research: Kapwing, 21% of first 500 Shorts pure AI slop plus 33% "brainrot." Raptive, trust down about 50% on perceived AI generation, ad premium impact down 17%.

Britain Cleared the Paramount-Warner Merger for Promises About Children's TV and Channel 5 News
Britain took no divestiture at all. It took commitments that Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network keep commissioning UK children's content and that Channel 5 News stays editorially separate from CBS News and CNN International.
CEO Summary
The UK cleared Paramount Skydance's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. on both competition and public interest grounds. The Competition and Markets Authority found no competition issues requiring intervention after examining theatrical film distribution, linear children's TV channels and subscription VOD supply, and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy declined to issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice in exchange for legally binding behavioral commitments. Paramount immediately cited the ruling against the US state attorneys general, whose case goes to trial in March 2027. The European Commission approved the deal on July 22.
Why This Matters
Paramount's same-day citation of the UK ruling against the state attorneys general treats a different legal standard as though it bears on this one. The CMA and Culture Secretary applied UK competition and public-interest tests to UK market structure, while the March 2027 California trial turns on US antitrust market definitions the UK proceeding never examined. The UK clearance is a public-relations data point for Paramount, not a precedent the US court has reason to weigh.
Specific Implication
Producers of UK children's content and UK news retain mandated commissioning at Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network and Channel 5 for as long as the clearance conditions bind.
The Facts
  • Transaction: Paramount Skydance's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros., cleared in the UK on competition and public interest grounds.
  • CMA finding: "no competition aspects of this proposed merger in the U.K. which necessitate their further intervention." Areas examined: theatrical film distribution, linear children's TV channels, supply of subscription VOD services.
  • Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy declined to issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice.
  • Commitments: no consolidation of UK linear channels with on-demand services, distinct editorial identity retained; Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network to remain editorially distinct and keep commissioning and acquiring original UK children's content; Channel 5 News editorially independent and separate from CBS News and CNN International; CNN International to remain available in the UK; licensees keep access to CNN, CBS News and Channel 5 news archives on standard commercial terms; Channel 5 to continue as a Public Service Broadcaster with a UK-focused commissioning strategy and more funding for news, original children's programming and drama.
  • Paramount statement: "These conclusions further demonstrate the misguided and gerrymandered market definitions relied upon by the U.S. state AGs in their antitrust complaint in California."
  • European Commission approved July 22, 2026.
  • US trial: March 2027, brought by California AG Rob Bonta with 11 other state AGs and the WGA.

An AI Startup Paid WGA Scale for a Black List Script and Licensed Four Real Likenesses for a 110-Minute Film
N3on gave a two-minute voice recording and some photos, and got "a pretty good check with very little work." The film runs 110 minutes.
CEO Summary
AI startup Higgsfield has made "Cully Hill Boys," a 110-minute film it says is the first AI-generated production featuring legally licensed celebrity likenesses: streamer N3on, UFC fighters Israel Adesanya and Quinton "Rampage" Jackson, and basketball influencer Matt Kiatipis. The screenplay was purchased from the Black List submission service, and writer Tim Planagan, who is not a WGA member, said his fee was "on par" with WGA rates under a grant limited solely to AI adaptations. The film is not intended for commercial release; Higgsfield built it to showcase its Cinema Studio platform to studios.
Why This Matters
Structuring the grant as "AI adaptation" rather than a defined right under an existing WGA category let Higgsfield pay a rate it characterizes as scale to a non-guild writer without the deal touching guild minimums or successor protections at all. Those protections attach to specific enumerated rights, not to an open-ended AI label. That structure is available to any buyer negotiating with a guild writer directly, not just with non-members like Planagan.
Specific Implication
The rates reported here, a non-WGA writer's AI-adaptation-only grant and a minimal-input likeness license, were set in a technology showcase with no commercial release and non-A-list participants. Representatives negotiating a comparable AI-adaptation or AI-likeness grant for a guild writer or higher-profile talent should treat this deal as a floor reference point, not a market rate.
The Facts
  • Film: "Cully Hill Boys," 110 minutes, directed by Aitore Zholdaskali, who also directed Higgsfield's "Hell Grind."
  • Licensed likenesses: N3on (Mikyle Rafiq, 21), Israel Adesanya, Quinton "Rampage" Jackson, Matt Kiatipis. Variety reports it as the first AI-generated production with legally licensed celebrity likenesses.
  • Likeness input per N3on: a two-minute voice recording and some photos. He described "a pretty good check with very little work."
  • N3on audience: 1.1 million YouTube subscribers, roughly 700,000 on Kick.
  • Screenplay: purchased from the Black List submission service. Writer Tim Planagan is not a WGA member; his fee was "on par" with WGA rates and the grant was limited solely to AI adaptations.
  • Planagan previously declined producers who offered WGA rates but wanted the story moved from East London to the United States.
  • Purpose: a showcase for Higgsfield's Cinema Studio platform, not a commercial release.
  • Context: the WGA has an active #AINeedsHumans campaign over AI models training on writers' work.

The World Cup Doubled Fox's TV Ad Sales and Fiscal-Year Revenue Hit $17.13 Billion
TV division ad sales rose 108 percent on the World Cup and quarterly profit still fell 3 percent to $696 million. Tubi crossed 110 million monthly users.
CEO Summary
Fox reported fiscal Q4 ad sales up 78% overall and 108% at the TV division on the FIFA Men's World Cup, with adjusted EPS of $1.79 on $4.2 billion revenue against consensus of $1.34 on $3.6 billion. Quarterly profit nonetheless fell 3% to $696 million. Full-year revenue reached $17.13 billion, up 5%. Lachlan Murdoch cited the launch of FOX One, Tubi's growth and the announced Roku acquisition, and said separately on the call that Fox will not amend its NFL deal before it expires after the 2029 season.
Why This Matters
A quarter where TV ad sales more than doubled and profit still fell means the World Cup's rights and production costs outran the incremental ad revenue it generated, not merely offset it. That makes the tentpole a net drag on quarterly profitability even as it drove the ad-sales headline. It is consistent with tentpole sports being carried for audience acquisition into Fox's ad-supported assets rather than for standalone quarterly return.
The Facts
  • Fiscal Q4 (April to June 2026); Fox's fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30.
  • Ad sales up 78% overall, up 108% at the TV division.
  • Quarterly profit: $696 million, down 3% year over year.
  • Adjusted EPS $1.79 on $4.2 billion revenue, against LSEG consensus of $1.34 on $3.6 billion. Revenue up 28% year over year.
  • TV division revenue $2.5 billion, up 45%. TV ad sales $755 million, up 108%.
  • Cable network programming revenue $1.67 billion, up 9%. Divisional ad sales $83 million, up 22%.
  • Distribution revenue $2.03 billion, up 7% from $1.94 billion. Content and other revenue $262 million, down more than 2% from $269 million. Corporate and other $161 million versus $63 million.
  • Full year: revenue $17.13 billion, up 5%. Distribution up 4%. Ad sales up 7%. Content and other up 4% on higher sports sublicensing.
  • Tubi: 110 million monthly users and its highest revenue quarter yet.
  • Murdoch: fiscal 2026 delivered "record top-line revenue which converted into record EBITDA," alongside the FOX One launch and the announced Roku acquisition.

Netflix Gets the Grand Theft Auto VI Trailer Six Hours Before YouTube Does
The extended look premieres on Netflix at 3 p.m. ET on August 27 and reaches Rockstar's own YouTube channel and website at 9 p.m. Netflix calls it first-of-its-kind.
CEO Summary
Rockstar Games said Thursday that "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look" will premiere on Netflix on August 27 at 3 p.m. ET and reach the official Rockstar YouTube channel and the Grand Theft Auto VI site at 9 p.m. ET the same day, giving Netflix a six-hour exclusive window on promotional footage for a game 13 years in development. Netflix described it as "a first-of-its-kind partnership." No financial terms were reported. Pre-orders opened in June at $79.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for the ultimate version.
Why This Matters
Rockstar routing the trailer through Netflix before its own YouTube channel and website reverses the standard sequencing, where a rights holder posts promotional material to owned channels first and lets third parties pick it up afterward. Ceding that first window to a distribution partner, on a title this anticipated, signals Rockstar valued Netflix's reach or platform association enough to subordinate its own channel's traffic for six hours.
Specific Implication
Owners of high-anticipation, pre-sold IP now have a precedent for negotiating an exclusive early-access window on promotional material with a distribution partner rather than releasing marketing simultaneously across owned and partner channels. The Rockstar-Netflix arrangement does not establish a market rate for such a window, since no financial terms were disclosed.
The Facts
  • Rockstar Games press release, Thursday: "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look will premiere on Netflix Thursday, August 27 at 3 p.m. ET and will also launch on the official Rockstar Games YouTube channel and the Grand Theft Auto VI site at 9 p.m. ET on August 27."
  • Netflix window: six hours exclusive. Netflix called it "a first-of-its-kind partnership."
  • No financial terms reported.
  • "Grand Theft Auto VI" has been in development for 13 years.
  • Pre-orders opened in June: $79.99 standard edition (digital or physical), $99.99 ultimate edition with premium vehicles, weapons, apparel and additional content.
  • Rockstar has described the launch version as "a single-player experience set in the biggest, most immersive evolution of the series yet," with no multiplayer or online component mentioned.
  • Rockstar Games is owned by Take-Two Interactive.

LinkedIn Brand Deals Went From $100 to $500,000 a Year and the Rule Is Keep Your Day Job
Brands used to offer LinkedIn creators $100 a post. One rep's clients now average $10,000 a month per deal, and his 50 creators have earned $15 million on the platform.
CEO Summary
LinkedIn, with 1.3 billion registered users, has become a paying creator platform: the number of creators on it nearly doubled between 2021 and 2025, and rates have moved from roughly $100 offers a few years ago to about $10,000 per month for a single brand deal, putting top creators near $500,000 a year across three or four brands. Eighty-three percent of 2026 sign-ups so far are Gen Z and time spent on content is up 10% year over year. The platform also introduced a "Seems like AI slop" flag last week and is retiring the AI post-enhancement tool it launched in 2023.
Why This Matters
Retiring the AI post-enhancement tool it launched in 2023 while brand rates on the platform are climbing toward six figures is LinkedIn reversing its own earlier product bet. The company is now treating verified, human-written content as the asset that supports its rising creator rates, and AI-assisted posting as a liability to that premium rather than a feature worth keeping.
Specific Implication
Talent building a presence on LinkedIn, including athletes and performers approaching a career transition, has a named-source basis for negotiating rate on verified reach into a targeted professional audience rather than on follower count.
The Facts
  • 1.3 billion registered users. LinkedIn does not break out monthly actives; Facebook and Instagram each run around 3 billion.
  • Creators on the platform nearly doubled between 2021 and 2025, per the company.
  • Rates: brands once approached creators with $100 offers. Aneesh Lal of Wishly Group says his clients now average $10,000 per month for a single deal, most work with three or four brands consistently, and can make around $500,000 a year. His 50 creators have earned $15 million from LinkedIn brand deals in total.
  • One brokered integration with AI sales platform Apollo.io produced more than 100 pieces of native LinkedIn and newsletter content.
  • 83% of 2026 sign-ups so far are Gen Z, the fastest-growing demographic. Time spent on content up 10% year over year. Video is among the fastest-growing formats.
  • LinkedIn added a "Seems like AI slop" flag button last week. Hari Srinivasan, product strategy lead for core member experiences: "People come to LinkedIn to connect with real people and share their real perspectives, ideas and expertise." The 2023 AI post-enhancement feature is being replaced by a proofreading tool.
  • Lal: "I believe the best LinkedIn creators are not full-time creators."
  • Josh Kaplan of Smooth Media: brands can verify from a video's comments that it reached senior executives at target companies, which is pushing LinkedIn deal rates toward parity with other platforms.
  • Arrivals: Lisa Rinna (joined in spring, made a career-advice video with the platform), Grimes under her real name Claire Boucher, Steph Curry, Chris Paul, Alex Pall of The Chainsmokers. Curry posts more about his Underrated Golf tour and foundation than his NBA career.
  • Media companies incubating on the platform: Breaking & Entering (40,000+ followers on its main page, about 100,000 across all platforms) and TBPN.

Nielsen Is Buying DoubleVerify for $2.15 Billion to Fix the Thing Advertisers Stopped Trusting It On
Nielsen is paying $2.15 billion, a 30% premium, for DoubleVerify in an all-cash deal closing by Q1 2027, taking both the measurement and verification layers of the ad market private under one owner.
CEO Summary
Nielsen agreed to acquire ad-verification firm DoubleVerify for approximately $2.15 billion in an all-cash transaction, a 30% premium to DoubleVerify's 60-day trading average. The deal, approved by both boards, is expected to close by Q1 2027 and takes DoubleVerify private under Nielsen, which has itself been privately held since 2022. Providence Equity Partners, holding roughly 11.8% of DoubleVerify's shares, has agreed to vote in favor and will exit its stake at closing.
Why This Matters
DoubleVerify's commercial value to advertisers rested on being structurally independent of the measurement firms it checks. Folding it into Nielsen removes that independence, converting a third-party check on Nielsen's own data into a subsidiary of the company being checked. The "single currency" both CEOs describe only holds credibility with advertisers if the scoring stays separable from the measurement it grades, which common ownership makes harder to demonstrate, not easier.
Specific Implication
Counterparties with ad-based bonus, threshold, or revenue-share terms tied to Nielsen measurement should specify the underlying methodology and add a change-of-control or methodology-change clause to future contracts. The verification function historically cited to support those terms will no longer sit with an independently owned company.
The Facts
  • Nielsen will acquire DoubleVerify in an all-cash transaction valuing the company at approximately $2.15 billion, or $13.60 per share, a 30% premium to its 60-trading-day volume weighted average price as of August 5, 2026.
  • DoubleVerify shares rose nearly 14% in after-hours trading on the news.
  • The transaction has been approved by both boards and is expected to close by Q1 2027, subject to DoubleVerify shareholder and regulatory approval; DoubleVerify becomes a private unit of Nielsen.
  • Providence Equity Partners, holding approximately 11.8% of DoubleVerify's outstanding shares as of August 5, has agreed to vote in favor and will exit its stake at closing.
  • Nielsen CEO Karthik Rao said the deal will "ensure that the spend flowing between buyers and sellers is reaching real people in brand-suitable environments, through verified channels." DoubleVerify CEO Mark Zagorski said the goal is "a single currency that scores media on both audience delivery and media environment quality."
  • Rival iSpot last week revealed an expanded pact with Fox providing advertisers real-time data on business outcomes such as car-showroom visits.

CEO Summary
LightShed Partners calculated from both companies' own Q2 2026 earnings-call guidance that Warner Bros. Discovery, ramping to 19 films in 2027 from 14 this year, and Paramount, on track for 15-plus films in 2027, would together release 34-plus theatrical films next year if they remain separate. Paramount has publicly committed to only 30 films annually if its acquisition of WBD closes. The note also cites Nexstar CEO Perry Sook's and Paramount CLO Makan Delrahim's public comments this week, and reiterates that the merger agreement expires June 4, 2027 with a $7 billion break fee owed, ahead of a March 2 trial.
Why This Matters
Sook is himself pursuing his own consolidation, the Nexstar-Tegna merger currently enjoined by eight state attorneys general. That makes his warning about a combined Paramount/WBD's affiliate leverage self-interested testimony rather than a neutral competitive read. A bigger Paramount/WBD is a rival broadcast-content supplier to the same station groups Nexstar is trying to enlarge. Sook benefits from any regulatory friction that slows a competitor's scale even as he seeks the same kind of scale for Nexstar.
Specific Implication
Producers, financiers, or filmmakers planning a 2027 theatrical release tied to either studio should treat the 30-films-per-year figure Paramount has committed to post-merger as the planning ceiling if the deal closes. The higher combined slate the two companies are guiding to applies only if they remain separate entities.
The Facts

  • Nexstar CEO Perry Sook told his own Q2 call that a combined Paramount/WBD "looks to have increased scale and resources to further pressure broadcast affiliates to pay more for less content."
  • Paramount CLO Makan Delrahim argued on LinkedIn for a federal preemption model over state-by-state merger review; JPMorgan is helping finance the WBD/Paramount transaction.

Netflix Spends 5 Percent of Its Content Budget on 1 Percent of Its Viewing Because Live Cannot Be Faked

CEO Summary
Netflix devoted roughly $1 billion, about five percent of its 2026 content budget, to live programming that generates only about one percent of total viewing hours, The Ankler reports. Co-CEO Greg Peters said on the July earnings call that live events drove six of the ten biggest new-subscriber sign-up days in the past five years. Producers behind recent Netflix live events, including Plimsoll's Skyscraper Live and Done+Dusted, describe a broader industry shift toward live formats as the one content category that cannot be synthetically generated.
Why This Matters
Whisper TV hiring native speakers to dub the Fury-Makhmudov fight for each international feed, instead of using AI translation on a marquee live event, shows the AI-proof premium on live extends past production into localization. Even the category treated as immune to synthetic generation is being kept manually produced end to end for its highest-value broadcasts, not just at the point of capture.
Specific Implication
Producers capable of delivering complex live formats, spanning multiple time zones, insured, and multilingually produced, are operating from a narrower supply base than Netflix's spending growth alone would suggest. Banijay has been building its dedicated live division since 2023.
The Facts
  • Live accounts for roughly one percent of Netflix's viewing hours; Netflix devoted approximately $1 billion, about five percent of its 2026 content budget, to it.

CEO Summary
Roku reported Q2 2026 profit of $164.2 million, or $1.08 per share, up 1,464% year over year, on revenue up 22% to $1.35 billion, beating Wall Street's 56-cent consensus. Platform revenue, 90% of the total, grew 25% with ad revenue up 39%. Why This Matters
The redesigned home screen finishing its U.S. rollout to more than half of broadband households just ahead of close means Fox is acquiring a placement platform Roku's own management has already built and deployed. It is not one Fox will have to develop after the deal closes. Roku's record quarter, and the ad and subscription growth built on that home screen, becomes evidence of what Fox is buying rather than a basis for shareholders to seek better terms. The acquisition price was fixed before this performance was reported.
Specific Implication
Programmers negotiating carriage or placement on Roku's home screen should treat current terms as provisional pending Fox's ownership change, since Roku disclosed no guidance on how placement decisions will be handled once the acquisition closes.

Gareth Edwards Directed an $869 Million Jurassic Film and Universal Is Replacing Him Anyway
Gareth Edwards, whose Jurassic World: Rebirth grossed $869 million, will not direct the sequel over creative differences; David Koepp's script and stars Scarlett Johansson, Mahershala Ali and Jonathan Bailey are already locked, and a new director search is underway.
CEO Summary
Gareth Edwards will not return to direct the next Jurassic World film after creative differences with Universal, TheWrap reports, despite his 2025 film Jurassic World: Rebirth grossing $869 million globally. David Koepp has already written the follow-up script, and stars Scarlett Johansson, Mahershala Ali and Jonathan Bailey are expected to return; a new director search is underway. A Universal-side insider described the franchise as having rotated through five different core casts and directing teams across seven films, with producers Steven Spielberg and Frank Marshall as the constant.
Why This Matters
An $869 million global gross did not secure Edwards a renewed mandate. Box office return on the prior entry is therefore not itself the qualifying criterion for keeping a director on this franchise. Alignment with the producers who hold actual continuity, Spielberg and Marshall, functions as the higher bar. A director weighing a future Jurassic assignment should read a strong opening for the franchise as necessary but not sufficient for a second film.
Specific Implication
Directors accepting an assignment on an established franchise where script and cast are set independently of them should negotiate first-position or script-input terms before signing. Box office results on a prior entry did not carry over into creative continuity on this franchise.
The Facts
  • Gareth Edwards will not return to direct the next installment in the Jurassic World franchise, citing creative differences, TheWrap reported.
  • Edwards directed 2025's Jurassic World: Rebirth, which grossed $869 million globally.
  • Universal statement: "We had an incredible experience working with Gareth on 'Jurassic World Rebirth.'"
  • A script for the follow-up has already been written by David Koepp. Stars Scarlett Johansson, Mahershala Ali and Jonathan Bailey are expected to return, and a director search is underway.
  • An insider told TheWrap the franchise "has always evolved with different filmmakers and cast," with continuity resting on Spielberg and Marshall.
  • Edwards also directed Rogue One and The Creator.

A deal being negotiated with WBD while the merger is pending is subject to Paramount's consent rights if its value or term falls within the stated thresholds. That affects how quickly it can close relative to a deal structured to fall outside them.
The Facts

  • Ordinary-course deals are restricted to lasting only two years past deal close; anything longer requires giving Paramount first rights to negotiate.
  • Separate limits apply to deals involving undefined "key property" IP (THR notes franchises like Harry Potter, Game of Thrones and DC likely qualify) and to HBO Max bundle agreements, both capped at two years post-closing.

The Paramount-WBD antitrust trial starts March 2, 2027, and the $7 million a day clock starts October 1

CEO Summary
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín set the trial over Paramount Skydance's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery for March 2 to March 19, 2027, closer to the April date sought by twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America than the November start Paramount requested. Paramount owes Warner shareholders a ticking fee of 25 cents per share per quarter, roughly $7 million a day, for every day the deal does not close after September 30, which the trades put above $1 billion by the time trial opens. The merger agreement expires June 4, 2027, and carries a $7 billion regulatory termination fee.
Why This Matters
Paramount's refiling exposure extends beyond the Justice Department, to the 65 jurisdictions worldwide it says have already cleared the deal or declined to challenge it. A trial date that slips past any of those regulators' own clearance windows could force Paramount to redo approvals it has already banked. That makes the March 2027 date a multi-jurisdiction risk rather than a single US antitrust question.
Specific Implication
Anyone planning around Paramount's stated ramp to 30 films a year should treat the trial calendar, not the ramp date itself, as the operative schedule until the merger closes.
The Facts
  • Trial set for March 2 to March 19, 2027, before U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland. Court hours 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m.; dark March 8 and March 15.
  • Paramount sought a November 2026 start. The state attorneys general and the WGA proposed April 2027.
  • Ticking fee: 25 cents per WBD share per quarter for every day past September 30 the deal has not closed, roughly $7 million per day, more than $1 billion by trial.
  • Merger agreement expires June 4, 2027. Regulatory termination fee: $7 billion.
  • A Justice Department waiting period expires February 19, 2027; Paramount told the court a later trial forces refiling in the United States and other cleared jurisdictions.
  • California Attorney General Rob Bonta leads 11 other state AGs. Suit filed July 13, followed by a temporary restraining order.
  • Initial case management conference August 19; joint statement due August 13. No timeline given for a post-trial ruling.

  • On the same day's earnings call, CEO David Ellison said he is "absolutely open" to settling but expects to win at trial.
  • Paramount told the court it plans to raise output to 30 films per year and that the later date prolongs uncertainty for the creative community.

TV Media revenue fell 9 percent to $3.1 billion while its profit grew, and the company raised full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to $3.8 billion to $3.9 billion with cost savings now expected above $2.7 billion.
Why This Matters
Paramount's two segments moved in opposite directions this quarter. TV Media revenue fell 9 percent to $3.1 billion while segment profit grew. The company attributed that combination in part to lapping the NCAA tournament and the Telefe and Chilevision sales rather than to a change in the underlying business. Paramount+ reached its best retention quarter on record, which the company tied to Dutton Ranch, UFC and non-exclusive World Cup rights held in six Latin American markets, rather than to exclusive licensing. The results were reported while the WBD merger remains pending trial, with Ellison telling shareholders the company "fully expect[s] the transaction to close."
The Facts
  • Q2 total revenue about $6.9 billion, flat year over year, in line with forecasts. Full-year 2026 revenue expectation: $30 billion.
  • Net profit $41 million, down from $57 million.
  • Paramount+ reached 81.6 million subscribers worldwide, up about 2 million; lowest quarterly churn in the service's history. BET+ was folded into Paramount+ in the quarter.
  • DTC revenue $2.5 billion, up 9 percent. DTC profit $366 million, up 44 percent. Paramount+ advertising up 30 percent.
  • TV Media revenue $3.1 billion, down 9 percent, with segment profit up. Advertising down 14 percent, including about eight points from lapping NCAA tournament games and three from the Telefe and Chilevision sales. Affiliate revenue down 6 percent.
  • Studios revenue $1.3 billion, up 16 percent on third-party deliveries and consolidated Skydance licensing, against lower theatrical revenue lapping "Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning." Swung to $36 million profit from a $31 million loss.
  • Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance raised to $3.8 billion to $3.9 billion. Cost savings above $2.7 billion expected by year end; more than $3 billion in combination efficiencies still targeted.
  • PSKY closed at $8.38, up 1.95 percent; shares rose after the release, then reversed to down about 1 percent.
  • Ellison to shareholders: "we fully expect the transaction to close and remain focused on preparing for a successful combination once it is complete."
  • Ellison said 65 jurisdictions have cleared the WBD transaction or declined to challenge it, and that the combined company would hold 13.4 percent of U.S. television and streaming viewing time and 18 percent of domestic box office over the past 12 months.

Set against the $360 million opening weekend, the Monday result is meaningfully larger than the standard weekday drop-off for a film this size, where gross typically concentrates in the first three days. That weekday hold, more than the size of the opening itself, is what carried the film past $1 billion in six days.

Participation and bonus structures written against a three-day opening-weekend threshold would not have captured the scale of this film's post-opening performance, since a meaningful share of its gross accrued after the weekend closed.

Private equity is sitting on about $1 trillion and buying the parts of entertainment AI cannot copy
Apollo argued in a December white paper that sports hedges AI because the seats are finite and the games run live. KKR has $53 billion to deploy, Blackstone $43 billion.
CEO Summary
Roughly $1 trillion in uncommitted U.S. private equity capital is looking for somewhere to go, and reporting across lawyers, financial advisers and dealmakers found one thesis recurring: sports, live events and other scarce real-world experiences are being underwritten specifically because generative AI cannot replicate them. Private equity already holds positions across the representation and management business and in production, from a $25 billion Endeavor take-private to the $8 billion Banijay-All3Media merger. Firms target 18 to 20 percent annual returns on five-to-seven-year holds, and continuation vehicles that let original investors stay past a fund's expiry are now routine in media.
Why This Matters
That capital overhang functions as a driver independent of the AI-hedge thesis. Fund structures force deployment before an expiration clock, so dry powder needs a home whether or not a given target actually resists AI substitution. One dealmaker put the dynamic bluntly: "Money has to be invested, whether that money is a useful investment or not." A seller courted under the sports-and-scarcity narrative should weigh whether the buyer's real motive is thesis conviction or capital that simply has to move.
Specific Implication
A talent business or media asset acquired by a private-equity-backed platform should expect the platform's ownership horizon, typically five to seven years or extended via a continuation vehicle, to shape deal terms. The underlying thesis prices scarcity and live, in-person value specifically for eventual resale.
The Facts
  • Midyear estimates put uncommitted U.S. private equity capital near $1 trillion. One corporate dealmaker: "Money has to be invested, whether that money is a useful investment or not."
  • Typical targets: 18 to 20 percent annual returns, five-to-seven-year exits. Continuation vehicles, single-purpose funds letting original investors stay in, are increasingly common in media and entertainment as an alternative to expiry-driven fire sales.
  • Apollo Global Management: $67 billion in private equity; holds HarbourView, Legendary Entertainment and Wrexham AFC; launched Apollo Sports Capital in September; a December 2025 white paper argued sports hedges AI disruption because seats are finite and games are watched live. Took a minority Legendary stake for $760 million in 2022.
  • Silver Lake: $114 billion. Completed a $25 billion Endeavor take-private last year and is part of the $55 billion EA leveraged buyout with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Affinity Partners, cleared by EU regulators July 23.
  • KKR: $255 billion, about $53 billion available. Holdings span Mediawan, Simon & Schuster, Epic Games, ByteDance and Superstruct. Acquired Arctos this year; the only firm approved by all five major U.S. leagues to hold multiple team stakes.
  • Blackstone: $174 billion in private equity, $43 billion available as of June 30. Its $1 billion Candle Media bet has struggled since acquisitions of Hello Sunshine, Moonbug and ATTN.
  • RedBird Capital: $14 billion, dry powder about $965 million. Put $1.8 billion into Skydance's $8 billion Paramount purchase and committed $250 million toward the Paramount-WBD deal. RedBird IMI merged All3Media with Banijay for about $720 million in cash, creating the world's largest independent producer.
  • Providence Equity Partners is buying the remaining stake in The Team; at a reported $3.4 billion valuation the balance costs about $1.36 billion against just under $2 billion of dry powder.
  • EQT: $335 billion total; lost the auction for The Team and told Bloomberg it plans to invest $250 billion in the U.S. over five years. Shamrock Capital raised more than $800 million after selling its Excel stake.
  • Named new entrants circling the sector: Permira ($91 billion), Warburg Pincus ($105 billion, which hired a former major-label chief AI officer last year), Bluestone Equity Partners ($440 million).
  • One dealmaker on the consensus: "Everyone has dry powder for sports."

The WBD merger agreement forces Warner to sue over a departing executive, and California law punishes it for trying
Barlow's restriction runs to October 2027. Amazon's answer is that Warner is asking a court to bind her while reserving the right to change her owner, her reporting line and her job, with no promise of employment from the buyer.
CEO Summary
Warner Bros. Discovery has sued Amazon over its hiring of HBO Max marketing executive Pia Barlow before her fixed-term contract expired, calling Amazon a "digital bull in a china shop." The Paramount merger agreement bars WBD from failing to enforce employees' restrictive covenants, and a failure to enforce could hand Paramount an argument against paying the $7 billion regulatory termination fee if the deal is blocked, so WBD is pushed toward aggressive enforcement. California's 2024 amendments to Business and Professions Code §16600 cut the other way, requiring courts to read the noncompete prohibition broadly and giving an employee subjected to attempted enforcement of a void restraint their own claim for an injunction, damages and attorney fees.
Why This Matters
The merger agreement bars WBD from failing to enforce restrictive covenants, and non-enforcement could support a Paramount argument against paying the $7 billion termination fee. Together those supply a contractual reason for WBD to bring this suit independent of the underlying relationship with Barlow. The complaint's structure suggests an awareness of the risk on the other side: it does not name Barlow as a defendant, attach the employment agreement, disclose its termination terms, or seek emergency relief. That caution is consistent with California's 2024 amendments to Business and Professions Code section 16600, which let an employee facing enforcement of a void restraint sue for an injunction, damages and attorney fees. A comparable case last year, Disney's attempt to block Justin Connolly's move to YouTube, was denied emergency relief by a California judge and later settled.
Specific Implication
An executive departing a company mid-merger, where covenant enforcement may be contractually required rather than discretionary, should seek an explicit release as a condition of exit rather than rely on an assessment that the restriction is unenforceable.
The Facts
  • WBD sued Amazon over the hiring of HBO Max marketing executive Pia Barlow before her fixed-term contract expired; her restriction would run to October 2027.
  • The Paramount-WBD merger agreement prohibits WBD from waiving or failing to "enforce the restrictive covenant obligations" of current or former employees. Non-enforcement could support a Paramount argument against the $7 billion regulatory termination fee.
  • California's 2024 amendments to §16600 require courts to invalidate noncompetes "no matter how narrowly tailored" and remove the assumption that an unenforceable restraint carries no downside. Whether the statute voids a bona fide fixed-term contract is unsettled.
  • The same legislation lets an employee or former employee facing attempted enforcement of a void restraint sue for an injunction, actual damages and attorney fees.
  • Precedent: 20th Century Fox and Viacom defeated Netflix on executive poaching a decade ago. Last year Disney failed to block former ESPN executive Justin Connolly from joining YouTube; Judge James Chalfant refused emergency relief, found no probability of success, faulted Disney's showing of urgency, and held the balance of harms favored Connolly. Disney appealed; the parties settled before an appellate ruling.
  • Connolly's argument: because Disney could terminate him without necessarily paying the remainder, the deal looked less like security exchanged for a term commitment and more like a one-way noncompete.
  • WBD is represented by Proskauer partner Anthony Oncidi, who represented Viacom in the earlier case. He has not named Barlow as a defendant, attached the agreement, disclosed its termination provisions, or moved for emergency relief, and has emphasized Amazon's conduct, including its promise to absorb the legal consequences of her departure, its selection of counsel for her, and its alleged pursuit of other WBD executives.
  • WBD frames its interest as workforce stability and business planning; Amazon's position is that WBD is preparing to change owners, reporting structures and job definitions.

Ellison stayed silent from the July 13 suit until Tuesday's op-ed, which ran hours before Paramount's Q2 earnings call and while the judge weighs a November trial against April 2027.
CEO Summary
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison published a guest essay in the New York Times on Tuesday, his first public response to the antitrust suits filed by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America to block the $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. He argues the case is not about market share but about whether he can be trusted with CNN, writing that he has "regularly voted for candidates of both parties" and does not "aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views." The essay ran the same day Paramount reports Q2 results and while a federal judge weighs Paramount's request for a November 4 trial against the plaintiffs' request for April 5, 2027.
Why This Matters
Ellison's essay answers a question the antitrust case is not formally asking. The state attorneys general's and WGA's suit turns on market concentration, a competitive-effect standard. His response addresses his own trustworthiness on editorial matters, an argument aimed at political and public perception rather than at what a court will decide. The essay's silence on President Trump points the same way, toward a fight being waged as much in Washington and public opinion as in the courtroom.
The Facts
  • The suits were filed July 13 by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and 11 other state attorneys general, joined a day later by the Writers Guild of America. The transaction is valued at $110 billion.

  • On the substance: "I believe this fight is not really about market share … I believe a plainer worry sits beneath the briefs and the news releases: the news. The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner's CNN."
  • On his politics: "I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans."
  • On the commitments: "I don't ask to be taken at my word; the commitments are in writing, and the work will be on screens where anyone can judge it."

A leaked Microsoft memo obtained by The Verge shows the next Xbox, codenamed Project Helix, is built to run games from all five Xbox generations plus PC titles, which would give it the largest library of any home console. A judge threw out Terrence Howard's 'Empire' pay suit because his loan-out company would have been paid, not him
Fox contracted with Howard's loan-out, Universal Bridges, which paid him a fixed salary. The judge held that a higher fee would have raised the entity's revenue only, making damages too speculative for trial.
CEO Summary
Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Cherol Nellon dismissed Terrence Howard's 2023 suit against CAA on July 31, ending a case that had targeted packaging fees and alleged that conflicted advice cost him market-rate pay across six seasons of Fox's "Empire." The ruling turned on structure rather than conduct: Fox contracted with Howard's loan-out company, which paid him a fixed salary, so the court found that a successfully negotiated increase would have raised the loan-out's revenue without necessarily reaching him, making the alleged damages too speculative for trial. The court also found the agency did push Fox to renegotiate in 2018 and that Fox "rejected all attempts at renegotiation."
Why This Matters
The court's rationale does not touch Howard's core allegation, that CAA represented him alongside "Empire" co-creators Lee Daniels and Danny Strong and producer Imagine Entertainment without disclosing the conflict. The dismissal rests on the loan-out structure making damages too speculative. An artist with the same alleged multiple-representation conflict, but paid directly rather than through a fixed-salary loan-out, would face a different damages analysis. The merits question this ruling never reached would also be live for that artist.
Specific Implication
An artist compensated through a loan-out on a fixed internal salary, rather than one that passes through negotiated increases, should confirm which structure applies before pursuing a claim tied to underperformance of a deal. This ruling shows the structure itself can determine whether damages can be established.
The Facts
  • Judge Cherol Nellon, Los Angeles Superior Court, dismissed the suit on summary judgment in a ruling issued July 31, 2026.

  • Fox contracted with his loan-out, Universal Bridges, which paid him a fixed salary as an employee. Judge Nellon: "The immediate economic result of an increase in compensation would have been an increase in revenue to Universal Bridges only."
  • The court found alleged damages too speculative for trial, and separately found that the agency pushed to renegotiate while Fox held final say and "rejected all attempts at renegotiation."
  • The relationship soured in 2018 when his side sought profit participation, perks and promotional opportunities beyond the episodic fee; Fox declined to reopen the deal. Talks broke down again a year later over a request to raise the episodic fee from $325,000 to $750,000.
  • Claims brought: breach of fiduciary duty, constructive fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation.
  • A CAA spokesperson said the order made clear the uncontested evidence contradicted the foundation of the complaint, and that the agency sought to renegotiate with Fox in 2018 and Fox refused.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day opens to $927M worldwide and drives the biggest weekend in box office history
Sony's own public projection was $425M worldwide and roughly $200M domestic; the film did $927M worldwide and $355M domestic, about double the studio's guidance in each case.
CEO Summary
Sony and Marvel Studios' Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened to $355M domestic and $927M worldwide, the second-biggest global debut ever behind Avengers: Endgame. The entire North American market hit a record $428.99M for the weekend per Rentrak, the first all-time domestic weekend record since 2019. Sony's own public projection had been $425M worldwide, and Universal's three-week-old The Odyssey held at -43% alongside it rather than being crushed.
Why This Matters
The 24.1M domestic tickets sold represent about 20% more admissions than Spider-Man: No Way Home on a 27% larger nominal gross. That indicates the record reflects real audience growth rather than ticket-price inflation carrying the number. Admissions growth is the stronger signal for whether Marvel and Sony can sustain an audience this size at comparable pricing across future entries in the franchise.
The Facts
  • $355M domestic opening, second-best all time, roughly $2M behind Avengers: Endgame's $357.1M record. $927M worldwide across 90,000 screens, second-best global debut ever.
  • North American marketplace: record $428.99M weekend for all titles per Rentrak. Variety reported ~$430M and TheWrap $434M; the Rentrak figure is the measurement-of-record number. Prior all-time record was $402M (final weekend of 2019); best post-Covid weekend was $311.3M (July 2023).
  • Weekend was +246% against the same frame a year ago. YTD domestic box office is $6.19B through August 2, +15% year over year.
  • Sony's public global projection was $425M; The Ankler reports domestic guidance around $200M.
  • International: $572M from 66 markets. China $121.0M, UK $49.0M (#3 all time), Mexico $38.3M (#2), India $31.8M (best ever for a Hollywood picture there, sixth-biggest opening in Indian history), South Korea $25.0M, Australia $21.4M, Germany $20.0M, Italy $18.2M, Japan $10.0M. All-time like-for-like opening records also set in France, Brazil, Spain, Peru, Colombia, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Chile, Turkey, Ecuador and Belgium.
  • Production budget $225M (The Ankler). 24.1M US tickets sold per Entelligence against ~20M for Spider-Man: No Way Home — about 20% more admissions for a 27% larger nominal gross.
  • CinemaScore A. Opening-night audience 63% aged 18-34, 60% male; 36% White, 28% Latino, 20% Black, 10% Asian, 6% Native American/other.
  • Universal's The Odyssey took $51M in its third domestic weekend, -43%, for a $911M global cume.
  • MCU lifetime grosses now $33.3B across 38 films.
  • Rentrak's Paul Dergarabedian: "the likelihood of a $4 billion summer and a $10 billion year just went up exponentially."

Ellison may have built himself an exit from his own $111 billion Warner deal
Walking away costs Ellison $9.8B, a $7B breakup fee plus $2.8B to Netflix. Closing costs $113B, including $80B of fresh debt, against a standalone Paramount Skydance carrying $12B in net debt.
CEO Summary
David Ellison bypassed settlement talks with the state attorneys general and took the Paramount Skydance / Warner Bros. Discovery merger straight to trial, absorbing potentially $1B or more in ticking fees to do it. William Cohan's read is that the move is optionality rather than confidence: with a June 4, 2027 drop-dead date, Ellison now has eleven months in which he can decide the deal is no longer worth doing. The walk-away math is a $9.8B mistake, the $7B breakup fee to WBD plus $2.8B to Netflix, against a $113B one if he closes.
Why This Matters
Even fully combined, Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery would carry roughly $113B in market value, against Netflix's roughly $300B and Disney's roughly $167B. The transaction that resolves the antitrust trial does not by itself close the scale gap that made WBD a takeover target in the first place. That positions the combined company as a plausible acquisition target of its own once litigation clears.
Specific Implication
A counterparty transacting with Paramount Skydance during the pendency period should weigh the company's balance sheet, not the trial's outcome, as the constraint most likely to determine whether Ellison closes or walks.
The Facts
  • Drop-dead date in the merger agreement: June 4, 2027. Ellison chose trial over settlement, absorbing potentially $1B+ in ticking fees.
  • Walk-away cost: $9.8B ($7B breakup fee to WBD, $2.8B to Netflix). Close cost: $113B, including a fresh $80B of debt and $42.5B of equity at risk.
  • Standalone Paramount Skydance carries $12B of net debt; market capitalization roughly $8B. PSKY closed at $7.96 on July 31 and continues to hit fresh lows.
  • Comparative scale cited: Netflix ~$300B, Disney ~$167B. Combined PSKY+WBD ~$113B.
  • WBD shareholder outcome: $31.75/share ($31 offer plus 25 cents per quarter of ticking fees, September through June). Zaslav personally receives an additional $550M on close.
  • Sale-process sequence: Ellisons' first bid $19/share, declined; Revlon mode; Netflix merger agreement signed; Ellisons raised to $31/share cash, a 63% increase. Largest breakup fee ever, plus a personal Larry Ellison backstop on equity and debt.
  • Cohan's read on a broken deal: Zaslav would take the $7B fee, pay down debt to investment grade, and revert to the June 2025 split-up plan.
  • Paramount reports Q2 on August 4. Trial-date positions are far apart: Paramount seeks November, the state AGs and WGA seek April.

In the international markets where Brand New Day did have IMAX access, China, Japan and Korea, the format still captured 16% to 18% of each territory's opening despite carrying The Odyssey's continuing run at the same time. A release whose date lands during a competing title's premium-format exclusivity window can still recover a meaningful share of premium-format revenue by shooting natively for an alternate format, as Brand New Day did with ScreenX.

  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened on zero domestic IMAX screens. The Odyssey holds the domestic network until The End of Oak Street on August 14, and keeps the 70mm IMAX screens into September.

IMAX cume on the title is $221M**, the No. 3 IMAX title of all time and the fastest any film has reached $200M in the format. 70mm locations did $5.1M this weekend for a $27.6M cume, about 12% of the IMAX total.

Discovery's $110B merger sits paused for up to eleven months pending the state attorneys general's antitrust suit, and Oliver was explicit about the reason for the timing: "We have various prospective business daddies circling, no one fully willing to commit just yet."
Why This Matters
Oliver extended by exercising an existing option rather than negotiating a fresh term. That means the one-year fallback was already written into his prior HBO agreement before the merger's antitrust delay was known. Other WBD talent holding similar option-based renewals may already have this contingency available to them without having to reopen negotiations.
Specific Implication
Talent renegotiating a contract at a company with an unresolved change of control can match the contract term to the transaction's expected resolution date. That avoids committing to a multi-year term with an ownership group that is not yet fixed.
The Facts
  • Oliver picked up an option to extend by one year, through the end of 2027. His prior contract was due to expire at year's end. Typical renewals for the show have run three years.
  • The Paramount / WBD $110B merger is paused for up to 11 months pending the federal antitrust suit brought by state AGs.
  • Oliver on ownership: "We have various prospective business daddies circling, no one fully willing to commit just yet."
  • Oliver on the merger: "Nothing's happening, and everything has stayed the same. That's the only way that we can really move forward, total denial."
  • Oliver on leverage: "You always want to be exactly as much trouble as you are worth. So the more you are worth to them, the more trouble you can cause."
  • Last Week Tonight has delivered HBO 76 Emmy nominations and 32 wins since 2014, with three more nominations this year. Oliver: the Emmys "have built us some level of golden armor over the years."
  • Over 2 million viewers stream the weekly deep dives on YouTube alone.
  • On legal exposure: "They think their job is to stop us getting sued. We think their job is to make sure that when we are sued, we win."

A festival backup file left in production exposed 13,535 industry contact records
The cause was a plain-text backup left in the production environment, found via a public IoT search engine. A separate file held roughly 135,000 contacts Fowler says could seed phishing at scale.
CEO Summary
Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler found 666,369 Tribeca Festival records exposed online, spanning 2019 to 2026, after a plain-text backup file was left inside the production environment. One folder held 13,535 contact entries with names, addresses, phone numbers and emails for filmmakers and actors including Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Guillermo del Toro, Robert De Niro, Jennifer Lawrence and Angelina Jolie. The festival disputes the characterization, saying no talent had personal contact information disclosed and the records were largely public-facing business contacts; Fowler says he saw consumer email accounts in the file.
Why This Matters
Fowler's own base rate is that an organization rarely suffers a second incident within three to five years once one becomes a remediation priority. That suggests Tribeca is now the safer property in this category. The greater exposure sits with comparable festivals and markets that have not yet had a plain-text backup surfaced by a public search engine and so have not yet been forced to fix the underlying practice.
Specific Implication
A festival, market or submission platform that stores industry contact data typically does not carry standard breach-notification terms in its participation agreements. A party that routinely shares contact information with such platforms may want that language addressed at signing rather than after an incident.
The Facts
  • 666,369 exposed records, timestamps spanning 2019 to 2026, found via a publicly available IoT search engine.
  • Root cause per Fowler: "a human error of leaving the backup file in the database, and the backup file was in plain text, unencrypted."
  • One folder, "contacts," held 13,535 entries — names, addresses, phone numbers, emails. Cited: Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Guillermo del Toro, Ron Howard, Robert De Niro, Jennifer Lawrence, Angelina Jolie, Morgan Freeman, Rami Malek, Eva Mendes, Michael J. Fox.
  • A separate document held roughly 135,000 contacts, which Fowler assumes are mailing-list and event signups.
  • Festival statement: "None of the talent referenced in recent reporting had personal contact information disclosed. The vast majority of the information consisted of public-facing business contact information, including PR representatives, talent representatives, front office email addresses, information from the Festival website, and other information that was already publicly available. All information was removed promptly upon discovery."
  • Fowler's response: some contacts were managers or assistants, "but I saw a lot of consumer email accounts, like Google or Yahoo."
  • Fowler found no evidence anyone else accessed it, and credited the festival with responding "very fast and professionally."
  • Fowler on the AI multiplier: "you can feed it information and ask it to create a phishing email... and send it to 135,000 people, and somebody's going to open it."
  • Fowler's base rate: organizations that suffer a data incident "statistically don't have another one for three to five years since it becomes a primary focus."
  • Tribeca was co-founded in 2002 by De Niro, Jane Rosenthal and Craig Hatkoff. Its 25th-anniversary edition ran June 3-14, 2026.

A distributor assessing leak exposure for a large, heavily marketed tentpole has two recent cases in which a pre-release leak did not measurably affect opening-weekend gross.

A Stolen Screener Drive Turns Into a $105 Million Claim Against Netflix

CEO Summary
Writer-producer Simon Afram and his company Op-Fortitude sued Netflix in California federal court for at least $105 million after an unencrypted master of their unreleased WWII thriller "Fortitude," directed by Simon West and starring Nicolas Cage, was stolen from Netflix's Los Angeles office during an acquisition screening. Netflix says it does not bear the risk of loss for a film "delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards," and that it withheld investigation details after a demand for $165 million. The producers say they paused sales because any buyer must now be told the film was compromised before release.
Why This Matters
The producer delivered an unencrypted master to Netflix for an acquisition screening on verbal instructions to delete it afterward; ten days later it was stolen from Netflix's office along with other drives. Both sides agree the file was unencrypted and that it was stolen, per the complaint and Netflix's public statement. No written delivery, encryption, or risk-of-loss terms governed the handoff, and each side disputes who bears the resulting loss.

The producers' damages claim does not allege the film has leaked. It rests on the disclosure obligation the theft now creates with every future buyer, and the producers say they have paused sales as a result.
Specific Implication
A seller delivering an unreleased master for a buyer's internal acquisition screening should secure written delivery, encryption, and risk-of-loss terms before the material leaves its custody. Neither party in this dispute had such terms in writing.
The Facts
  • Suit filed Thursday in California federal court by Simon Afram and Op-Fortitude, seeking at least $105 million.
  • An unencrypted master copy was on one of several drives stolen from Netflix's Sunset Bronson Studios office last month; Netflix's investigation concluded the other drives were empty.
  • Netflix expressed interest after receiving promotional materials in December 2025 and requested a working cut in June.
  • Per the complaint, Netflix asked for the digital cinema package key so it could test the film internally. A producer hand-delivered the drive June 15, said the DCP was unencrypted, and instructed Netflix to delete the files after screening.
  • Netflix disclosed the theft ten days later. Sean Berney, head of film acquisitions, June 25: "This is a first for us. Unfortunately, someone stole a good amount of drives from our office desks this past week."
  • The suit says Netflix would not disclose whether it filed a police report and declined to involve the LAPD after the filmmakers filed their own.
  • Netflix says it stopped sharing investigation details after a law firm for Afram demanded $165 million for the film in what it called a "hostile attempt to extort money."
  • Netflix statement: it "disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards," notes it does not own the rights, and says it offered to monitor piracy sites.
  • The producers say they paused sales despite domestic and international interest.

California's COMPETE Act Would Put Theatrical Windows And Multi-Picture Deals Under Antitrust Law
AB 1776 extends the Cartwright Act to single-firm conduct for the first time in its 119-year history, and adds monopsonization liability that has passed the Assembly and Senate Judiciary Committee.
CEO Summary
California's AB 1776, the COMPETE Act, has passed the Assembly and the Senate Judiciary Committee and now sits with Senate Appropriations. It would extend the Cartwright Act to single-firm conduct for the first time in the statute's 119-year history, creating state liability for monopolization and, critically, monopsonization. Puck's Eriq Gardner reports the practices exposed run from theatrical windows to multi-film talent contracts to refusing to license content to competitors.
Why This Matters
Because AB 1776 would create state-law claims, they would sit outside the federal case law that has made monopsonization theories difficult to win in federal court. A buyer-side claim already rejected under federal antitrust doctrine could be refiled and survive under California law if the bill passes. That gives plaintiffs a second track around unfavorable federal precedent rather than a stronger version of the same track.
Specific Implication
If enacted, AB 1776 would expose standard theatrical-windowing and multi-picture contract structures to state antitrust claims in California regardless of the outcome of the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger review. The bill's monopsonization provision, aimed at buyer-side conduct, is not limited to studios or distributors.
The Facts
  • AB 1776, the Competition and Opportunity in Markets for a Prosperous, Equitable and Transparent Economy (COMPETE) Act, introduced by Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry on 2026-03-23.
  • Status: passed the Assembly, passed the Senate Judiciary Committee, referred to Senate Appropriations.
  • Would create state-law liability for monopolization, attempted monopolization, maintenance of monopoly power, and monopsonization.
  • Extends the Cartwright Act to single-firm conduct for the first time since its enactment 119 years ago.
  • Puck reports exposed conduct includes theatrical windows, multi-film talent contracts, and refusals to license content to competitors.

Discovery merger is blocked, and that his office has encouraged Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle out of court. In a separate Friday filing, Paramount asked for a 12-day antitrust trial starting Nov. 4, 2026, while the 12 state attorneys general and the WGA asked for April 5, 2027. Past Sept. 30, the deal costs Paramount a ticking fee of roughly $650M per quarter, or $7M per day.

Newsom's push for a settlement relies on a jobs estimate that is itself provisional pending the state's deeper Department of Economic Opportunity analysis due Aug. 18. The administration is thus weighing in on employment grounds ahead of its own office completing the underlying data. The governor's office is pressing Bonta toward settlement while Bonta continues to seek a later trial date and remedies beyond a CNN sale. The political and legal tracks inside California's own government are not yet aligned on this merger.

A counterparty with pending business tied to either company should treat Paramount's Sept. 30 fee trigger and the contested trial date, not the parties' public settlement posture, as the operative near-term calendar.

  • Remedy preference: Bonta has said the states want structural remedies, explicitly beyond a CNN sale: separate cable channels, a separate streaming service, a separate news channel or TV studio, a separate film studio.
  • Alleged concentration: 27% of wide-release theatrical distribution, 30% of anticipated blockbuster films, 27% of the basic cable bundle.
  • Jobs: LA County Board of Supervisors analysis found roughly 2,500 local and 6,000 global jobs at potential risk. A deeper Department of Economic Opportunity analysis on production workers is due Aug. 18.
  • Cleared: DOJ, WBD shareholders, the European Commission (conditioned on a UIP exit), plus Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, China, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, South Africa, Ukraine, Montenegro, New Zealand, North Macedonia, and FDI authorities in Spain, Germany, Slovenia, Belgium, Czechia, Italy, France and Romania. The UK CMA decides by Aug. 7.
