BAFTA Gives Itself Audit Power Over AI Use — Without Banning It
BAFTA sets no ban and no disclosure threshold; it can request documentation of AI use and human involvement case by case, with the film committee ruling on eligibility.
CEO Summary
BAFTA published its 2027 film awards rules with new AI language: the awards recognize "outstanding human achievement" regardless of the tools used, and BAFTA reserves the right to demand documentation of AI use and the extent of human creative involvement, with the film committee ruling on eligibility. There is no ban, no threshold, and no mandatory declaration at entry. Separately, casting directors will now vote in performance-category longlisting and nominations, and the Outstanding British Film longlist expands to 20.
Why This Matters
Reserving the right to "dig in a bit deeper" without publishing a threshold is the shrewd part of the design. Because no producer knows what triggers a request, every film must document its AI use and human creative involvement as if it will be asked. BAFTA gets a de facto universal documentation requirement without writing a rule that could be gamed at the margin or challenged as arbitrary, and it keeps full discretion over which films to examine. Audit power held in reserve disciplines behavior more broadly than any bright-line disclosure rule would.
The Facts
  • BAFTA published eligibility and voting changes for the 2027 film awards, characterized by Variety as small tweaks relative to AMPAS's recent Oscar changes.
  • The AI language. Having added "human achievement" to the rulebook last year, BAFTA has now added: the awards recognize "outstanding human achievement in originating, shaping and realising the final artistic outcome, regardless of the tools used to bring this work to life. Where the use of Generative AI or other digital tools is relevant to the consideration of the work, BAFTA reserves the right to request additional information regarding the nature of such use and the extent of human creative involvement."
  • BAFTA's executive director of awards and content said the addition gives BAFTA the "opportunity to just dig in a bit deeper if there's something we want to check," with the film committee ruling on eligibility. Asked whether a fully AI-generated film or performance could ever be nominated: it "would always be a human that picks up a BAFTA."
  • Outstanding British Film: longlist expands from 15 to 20 after round one; nominations stay at 10 (five by membership vote, five by jury).
  • Performance categories: BAFTA's casting chapter will now vote alongside the acting chapter in longlisting and nominations, to "increase the expertise" across 700+ candidates in four categories.
  • BAFTA is not following the Oscars in permitting multiple nominations for one performer in the same category — previously allowed, banned after a review, and retained as banned to "level the playing field."
  • Bullying and harassment: CIISA-alignment declarations remain mandatory for British categories; BAFTA now requests the information from all submitted productions, with a stated expectation it becomes a requirement in future years.
  • Key dates: entries open July 22; round one voting Dec. 4; longlists Jan. 7; nominations open Jan. 19; final voting Jan. 26; ceremony Feb. 21.

A Broadway Musical Grossing $1M a Week Is Now a Money-Loser — and Only Five New Ones Are Set for Next Year
Cats: The Jellicle Ball capitalized at up to $18M against Hadestown's recouped $11.5M and an arriving technical show capitalized up to $31M; only five new musicals are set for next year.
CEO Summary
Cats: The Jellicle Ball, the Tony-winning ballroom-competition revival, announced an August 8 closing after roughly five months on Broadway despite grosses hovering around $1 million a week and high attendance. The problem was average ticket price against elevated operating costs, not demand. Only five new musicals have been announced for next year.
Why This Matters
The mismatch in the Facts is the diagnosis: the cost drivers are collective, union rates, theater rent, materials inflation, while every producer response cited is individual, smaller casts, less automation, longer marketing runways. Individual retrenchment cannot move a collectively set cost base; it only lowers the ambition of what gets staged, which is how a market that can still fill seats ends up with a shrinking pipeline. Until owners, producers and the unions negotiate the cost structure jointly, as the composer's public letter urges, the economics will keep selecting for star vehicles and recognizable IP by default. That is the exact conditioning one producer in the piece identifies as unsustainable.
Specific Implication
With fewer new stage productions in the pipeline and cost pressure on shows without a star or established title, capture and screen rights on a successful production carry standalone value. Those rights should be negotiated as their own asset rather than included by default.
The Facts
  • Cats: The Jellicle Ball — the critically acclaimed revival restaging the musical as a queer ballroom competition — announced an Aug. 8 closing after roughly five months on Broadway. It won three Tony Awards but missed Best Revival.
  • Grosses were hovering around $1 million a week pre-Tonys, with high attendance. The company was told at a July 13 meeting that the show could not generate enough revenue to cover expenses.
  • THR's reporting locates the problem not in attendance but in average ticket price: the show could fill seats, but not at prices sufficient to cover elevated Broadway operating costs.
  • Capitalization comps in the piece: Cats: The Jellicle Ball up to $18M (described as relatively low for this era); Hadestown $11.5M, recouped, now in year seven; Paddington, a technical show arriving in spring, capitalized up to $31M.
  • Only five new musicals have been announced for next year.
  • Cost drivers cited: post-pandemic supply-chain and materials inflation, utilities, theater rent, and rising rates for actors, musicians, stagehands and creative teams. Musicals are hit hardest — larger casts plus an orchestra — while plays increasingly carry celebrities who can command higher prices.
  • A lead producer on a long-running Tony-winning musical, quoted: "I'm watching a lot of shows not quite find the audience that can sustain them… There have always been more shows that fail than succeed. I think the proportion right now feels distorted."
  • The show's composer wrote publicly on July 14: "Without action, Broadway risks rivaling Hollywood's empty soundstages: increasingly dark theatres where bold new work once lived," calling on theater owners, producers and union leaders to convene.
  • Producer responses so far are individual, not collective: fewer set pieces, less automation, smaller casts, longer marketing runways, discounted previews. One incoming musical's lead producer: "The amount of time that you have for your show to pick up has shortened."
  • On audience conditioning: "We've trained audiences that the shows of value are the ones with stars and recognizable IP, and so now we have to try to dig ourselves out of that behavior pattern because that's not sustainable either."

A Franchise Its Creators Lost Two Decades Ago Came Back — and Is Now Monetizing a Second Window

Why This Matters
The all-new scenes are what turn this from a repackaging into a template: the recovered rights are being used to manufacture new product against the old title, which is where reversion actually pays. A clawed-back franchise held passively is a trophy. The play demonstrated here treats each window as a distinct product carrying newly produced material, so the value of getting the rights back compounds with every release rather than resting on the original's catalog performance. That reframes what reversion clauses are worth negotiating for: not the library, but the license to keep making.
Specific Implication
New material produced for a second-window release, such as scenes shot specifically for a director's cut, should have its credit and compensation terms clarified separately from the terms governing the original theatrical release.

The Judge Grounded the Merger Pause in Theatrical Distribution, Not Cable or Streaming
The court found 27% wide-release share compelling evidence of harm, below the conventional 30% presumption threshold, and rejected streaming efficiencies as a defense in footnote 5.
CEO Summary
The court's written TRO order evaluated the Paramount-WBD merger on the market for distribution of wide-release theatrical films, not cable or streaming, and found the combined firm's 27% share "compelling evidence" of substantial market share despite sitting below the 30% presumption threshold. Footnote 5 rejected streaming-market efficiencies as a defense outright. The preliminary-injunction hearing is August 3; trial is unlikely before 2027.
Why This Matters
The order's unscrambling analysis cites consolidation of operations, sharing of business-sensitive information, and potential termination or reassignment of employees as what would make the deal impossible to unwind. That turns the merging parties' own integration planning into the evidence justifying the pause. It also sets a template: the more thoroughly two companies prepare to combine before closing, the stronger the case for stopping them. Future media mergers facing state challenges will therefore have to keep integration work frozen through litigation timelines that can run past a year.
Specific Implication
Companies that still distribute films in wide theatrical release now sit within a market a federal court has treated as legally distinct from streaming. That distinction is relevant to how any future theatrical-distributor merger is reviewed.

Brands Become TV's New Development Money — Paying Writers Fair-Market Rates As Studios Pull Back
A vertical series of 50-60 chapters costs $175,000-$225,000 to make, about ten hours of content for the price of a 30-second ad; one motorsport property booked $40M in brand deals.
CEO Summary
Consumer brands are now funding scripted development, scripts, writers, and concept work, not just non-scripted, entering pre-writing and taking producer roles. One production company has four brand-supported scripted projects including a NASCAR-set family drama for Prime Video, and an audio-equipment giant launched its own entertainment studio in June. The backdrop: streamers ordered 24% fewer scripted titles in H1 2025 than a year earlier.

The norm in the Facts table is the tell. In non-scripted, brands typically fund at least half the production bill to earn a say in development. In scripted, the participation fee is negotiable and executives do not expect brand financing at tens-of-millions scale. Brands are buying the cheapest point of control in the value chain, development itself, where a modest check shapes what exists before any studio or streamer weighs in. That means brand influence over scripted content will run far ahead of brand dollars in it, and the standard tools for measuring sponsor involvement, which key off financing share, will understate it.
Specific Implication
Writers and producers evaluating brand-funded scripted development should confirm where final creative approval sits before agreeing to terms, since the brand's marketing objective enters upstream of the standard studio development process.

Thousands of Crew Flagged for Removal From the Industry Roster, With the Numbers That Explain Why
IATSE hours fell 36% since 2022 and $40M+ starts fell 37% since 2021; staying on the roster took one union day in three years, rejoining now needs 30 days in one.
CEO Summary
A few thousand IATSE members have been flagged for removal from the Industry Experience Roster, the preferred-hire list covering ~47,000 West Coast freelance crew, in the first enforcement round since 2022. Staying on required one day of union work in three years; getting back on requires 30 days in one year. The context: IATSE hours fell 36% from 2022 to 2025, and $40M+ U.S. live-action starts fell 37% from 2021 to 2025.
Why This Matters
The asymmetry between the exit and re-entry standards makes removal functionally permanent. In a market with a third fewer hours worked, thirty qualifying days in a single year is close to unattainable for the people who could not find one day in three. The roster therefore operates as a ratchet that converts a cyclical production downturn into permanent capacity loss. Because the eligibility terms were negotiated by the unions themselves with the AMPTP, the mechanism doing the converting is one IATSE signed. That is the harder problem it carries into the 2027 renegotiation than the removals themselves.
Specific Implication
A production planning a domestic shoot before the 2027 renegotiation should budget for a smaller pool of roster-listed experienced crew, since flagged members face a 30-days-in-one-year path back onto the list.

ItemDetail
The listThe Industry Experience Roster, administered by a nonprofit founded under collective bargaining agreements since 1965. Tracks West Coast freelance crew (grips, makeup artists, plumbers) with role experience. Employers agree in union contracts to hire from it first.

RequalificationReapply and requalify from scratch, which for many classifications means 30 days on eligible productions in one year versus the one-day-in-three that maintained status.

The Premium-Format Ceiling: Only 41 IMAX 70mm Screens Exist Worldwide, and the Projectors Can't Be Rebuilt
No new IMAX film projector has been built in about 50 years and IMAX no longer holds a complete manufacturing blueprint; a year of scavenging produced a net gain of just eleven screens.
CEO Summary
Only 41 IMAX 70mm locations exist worldwide, 25 in the US, for the current Universal release, and demand has some theaters sold out into the fifth week. No new IMAX film projectors have been built in about 50 years; many parts no longer exist, and IMAX no longer holds a complete manufacturing blueprint. A year of scavenging units and training 60 projectionists from scratch produced a net gain of eleven screens.
Why This Matters
The binding constraint is capital allocation, not projector scavenging. Per the Facts, exhibitors are declining to build auditoriums that can house 1.43:1 screens on construction cost, and the IMAX-AMC agreement directs new investment toward IMAX With Laser conversions instead. Scarcity in the film format is therefore being locked in by where exhibition money flows. That makes IMAX 70mm allocation a permanent, non-expandable premium that a filmmaker with sufficient leverage can contract for, and that studios will increasingly compete over as a fixed pool rather than a growing one.
Specific Implication
Screen count and hold-length commitments for IMAX 70mm engagements involve a fixed, scarce resource and can be negotiated as specific terms in a distribution agreement rather than assumed.

The Indie Completion-Bond Market Just Went From Two Players to One
A director-led feature that premiered at Tribeca 2026 was financed, bonded, produced and post-supported entirely inside the same combined group, and is now seeking distribution.
CEO Summary
Film Finances International is acquiring Media Guarantors, combining the two largest completion-bond guarantors for independent film under one company inside the STX Entertainment and Film Services International family. The group also finances, physically produces, and posts films, and says it will invest in data-driven risk-assessment tools to speed bond issuance.
Why This Matters
A completion bond is worth paying for precisely because the guarantor is independent of the production it polices. When the sole remaining guarantor also finances, shoots and posts the same films, the instrument drifts toward self-insurance, and its certification value to outside financiers weakens accordingly. The counterweight in the Facts, a niche market where most films avoid bonding and smaller vendors are struggling, means no competitive check is likely to re-emerge on its own. What a bond certifies going forward is therefore less third-party oversight of completion risk than the group's confidence in its own pipeline.
Specific Implication
Financing arranged outside a studio should have its completion bond priced independently, without a clause tying bond issuance to using the same group's production or post-production services.

Public and Commercial Broadcasters Pool Streaming Inventory in Germany — Former Rivals Combining Against the Global Platforms
ProSieben carried ZDF's content without an agreement, lost in court, and is now carrying it anyway under a formal deal starting Q4 2026, free and without ads.
CEO Summary

It joins a wave of similar moves: Channel 4 in talks with the BBC, TF1 onto Netflix, France Televisions onto Prime Video, and Disney+ content deals with four European broadcasters.
Why This Matters
The common structure across these pacts, carriage of existing catalogs with no joint commissioning, is the part that cuts against producers: distribution reach gets pooled while programming demand does not grow. Unlike a merger, no combined entity emerges with a larger commissioning budget, so the licensing buyer set per territory shrinks with nothing offsetting it. The State Media Treaty's encouragement of exactly this cooperation signals that European regulators will keep blessing consolidation in this form precisely because it stops short of formal combination.

Counterparties in active deals with either company should treat the August 3 preliminary-injunction hearing, not the merger's original closing timeline, as the operative date for the litigation's effect on the companies' near-term posture.

  • The TRO responds to the antitrust suit filed by California AG Rob Bonta and 11 other state AGs, arguing the combined firm would hold outsized market share in wide-release theatrical distribution, top-grossing-film distribution, and basic-cable-channel licensing.

  • Judge waived Paramount/WBD's usual bond/security requirement given the "public's vital interest in antitrust enforcement."

Bonta: "This is a critical first win in our case to ensure this megamerger never sees the light of day." NY AG Letitia James echoed the consumer-harm framing.

CEO Summary
Twelve state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, sued to block Paramount Skydance's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, a month after the DOJ cleared the deal. A federal judge heard the TRO motion Friday and will rule by July 22, the same day as the EU's provisional approval deadline. The suit alleges the combined company would control roughly 30% of anticipated top-grossing theatrical films.
Why This Matters
Paramount's defense, that the combined company is needed to compete with Netflix, answers a theatrical-concentration claim by pointing to a streamer, a move that treats theatrical and streaming as a single competitive market. The case therefore turns less on the share arithmetic than on whether the court accepts that market definition. If it does, the theatrical figures lose force. If it does not, Paramount is left defending concentration in exactly the markets the complaint defines, with its committed 30-plus films a year reading as a behavioral concession that the concern is real.
Specific Implication
Until the court rules and the acquisition closes, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery remain separate companies for contracting purposes. Agreements executed before a ruling or close are made with the entity that exists at signing, not with a post-merger combined company.
The Facts
A coalition of 12 state attorneys general (led by California's Rob Bonta) filed an antitrust suit on 2026-07-13 in the US District Court for the Northern District of California seeking to block Paramount Skydance's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery — a month after the DOJ cleared the deal. The suit alleges Clayton Act violations across three markets: wide-release theatrical distribution, "anticipated top-grossing" theatrical distribution, and basic-cable-channel licensing to distributors — a combined Paramount/WBD would hold ~27% share of wide-release theatrical distribution and control ~30% of anticipated blockbuster films. On Friday 2026-07-17, a federal judge heard 80 minutes of argument on the states' TRO motion and said she'd rule by July 22 — the date Paramount's counsel says the deal will not close by regardless. The EU has its own provisional approval deadline of July 22; the UK CMA has an open investigation. Paramount calls the suit "wrong on both the facts and the law" and argues the combined company is needed to compete with Netflix; Paramount's CEO has committed to 30+ films/year post-close.

CEO Summary
A24 is offering "Backrooms" director Kane Parsons, 21, a three-year first-look deal estimated around $65M, its largest offer ever to an individual director, to keep him from Warner Bros., HBO, Universal, and Amazon MGM, all actively courting him. Why This Matters
The structure of the A24 offer is the tell. The headline value rests on performance bonuses tied to two films that do not yet exist, which makes the reported number largely contingent rather than guaranteed compensation. The bidding war is therefore inflating quoted deal sizes faster than committed money, and the studios are buying option value on an audience pipeline rather than paying present-day rates for a proven filmography.
Specific Implication
Representatives of early-career genre filmmakers with a breakout result can cite these offers as comps for multi-picture, first-look money before a second film exists.
The Facts
"Backrooms" director Kane Parsons (21, whose $10M film is A24's top-grossing release ever at $374M global) is being courted by multiple studios for his next projects. Warner Bros. film chiefs flew to meet him in person to pitch an overall deal spanning film and TV; he then took a meeting with HBO leadership, since the Warners pitch bundles film and TV. Universal's chief has also met with him, fresh off winning "Obsession" director Curry Barker for his next film. Separately, Barker's "Obsession" follow-up is already shot at a Universal specialty label; mid-"Obsession"'s $400M run, a rival studio offered him $10M sight-unseen for his next original, but he stayed within the Universal family for his third film in what was described as a rich eight-figure deal. Midjourney Escalates Bid to Force Disney, Universal & Warner Bros. to Reveal Their Own Internal AI Use
A magistrate judge had limited discovery to consumer-facing AI tools; Midjourney's renewed motion seeks the studios' internal training data, model weights, board presentations and employee prompts.
CEO Summary
Midjourney renewed its motion to force Disney, Universal, and Warner Bros., the studios suing it for copyright infringement, to turn over records of their own internal AI use, including training datasets, model weights, board presentations, and every prompt studio employees have entered into Midjourney itself. A magistrate judge had limited discovery to consumer-facing AI applications. The studios call the motion a "fishing expedition."
Why This Matters
Midjourney's argument, that the studios are withholding documents showing whether they use unlicensed-trained AI internally, converts the infringement claim into a symmetry test. If discovery runs both directions, the plaintiffs' own internal AI practices become part of the price of pressing the case. That raises the settlement value of the dispute independent of the merits and explains why the fight over discovery scope has become the case's center of gravity.
Specific Implication
If the motion succeeds, the studios' internal AI practices would enter the public docket in that litigation. That disclosure would be directly relevant to any counterparty negotiating AI provenance or consent language with Disney, Universal, or Warner Bros.
The Facts
Disney and Universal sued Midjourney for copyright infringement over its models' ability to generate copyrighted characters; Warner Bros. filed a consolidated suit months later. A magistrate judge ruled in June that the studios only have to produce discovery on "consumer-facing" AI applications. Midjourney's July filing sought to overturn that limit, arguing the studios are withholding documents that would show whether they use unlicensed-trained AI internally — the same conduct they're suing Midjourney over. Per later reporting, Midjourney renewed the motion the week of 2026-07-13, now seeking internal AI business plans, training datasets, model weights, board-level presentations, and every prompt studio employees have entered into Midjourney itself. The studios' lead attorney calls it a "fishing expedition." The matter is in active discovery.

DGA, WGA & SAG-AFTRA Jointly Protest Emmys' Decision to Cut Five Categories From the Main NBC Telecast

The Television Academy voted to move five categories off the main NBC Emmy telecast on Sept. 14 to the earlier Creative Arts ceremonies, cutting the show from 24 to 19 televised awards. The cuts hit limited-series supporting acting, writing, and directing, plus variety-series writing. The DGA, WGA, and SAG-AFTRA issued a joint statement protesting the move.

The Academy justified the cuts by the telecast's fixed three-hour runtime, which frames broadcast minutes as the scarce asset being reallocated. The residual-waiver leverage described in the reporting, and its 2023 precedent, indicate the category cuts are not necessarily final pending further guild action.

The main show drops from 24 to 19 televised categories; the Academy cites limited three-hour runtime. The DGA, WGA, and SAG-AFTRA issued a joint statement calling the move a decision that "devalues the contributions of the talented people" the ceremony exists to honor. The guilds retain real leverage: they can decline to waive residual fees normally waived for main-telecast clip usage, contingent on a minimum category count per craft — the same lever that forced a public reversal in 2023 when a similar WGA protest succeeded.

The Paramount-WBD Fight Comes Down To One Question: What Counts As A Blockbuster
Paramount cited Obsession, made for $750,000 and grossing near $430 million, as proof the market is open; a ticking fee of roughly $650 million per quarter starts Oct. 1 if unclosed.
CEO Summary
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín heard the state AGs' emergency motion against Paramount's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Friday and will rule in writing before July 22, the date of an anticipated EU greenlight and the earliest possible close. The hearing turned on what counts as a blockbuster: Paramount cited the $750K creator film Obsession grossing $430M as proof the market is open; the states answered that five majors make blockbusters consistently. A ticking fee of roughly $650M per quarter starts Oct. 1.
Why This Matters
The most revealing detail is the rejected remedy. Paramount pushed to settle pre-filing with behavioral commitments, including 30 movies a year at a 45-day theatrical window, and the states refused anything short of structural separation. That refusal defines the endgame. The states are not negotiating for output guarantees, so no windowing or volume concession Paramount can offer resolves the case. It can only end in a divestiture, a court loss for the states, or Paramount absorbing the delay cost until one of those arrives.
Specific Implication
A counterparty negotiating output, windowing, or distribution terms with Paramount or Warner Bros. Discovery should treat the ruling due before July 22 as the operative date. That ruling, not either party's own stated timeline, determines whether either company's negotiating position or deal capacity changes.
The Facts
ProceedingFriday hearing before U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín (N.D. Cal., Oakland) on the state AGs' emergency motion for a TRO / preliminary injunction against Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery
Ruling timingJudge will issue a written ruling before July 22 — the date of an anticipated EU antitrust greenlight and the earliest the merger could theoretically close
Deal size$110–111B (sources vary); 12 states led by California AG Rob Bonta
Markets allegedThree: blockbuster films, wide-release movies, and cable networks
Ticking feeThe controlling shareholders agreed to pay 25 cents cash per share per quarter — roughly $650M per quarter, cited as ~$7.2M/day (Deadline) and ~$6.9M/day (THR) — to WBD shareholders for each day the deal is unclosed starting Oct. 1
Paramount's offerCounsel offered to forgo closing early if the court rules on a preliminary injunction by early September; the AGs asked for proceedings next year
States' share claimCombined company would take more than a quarter of every box office dollar; ~30% share of blockbuster distribution
Rejected remedyParamount pushed to settle pre-filing with behavioral commitments including 30 movies a year at a 45-day theatrical window; the states refused, wanting structural relief (separating a film studio, cable channels, or a news channel)

The hearing's central exchange was definitional. Paramount's counsel cited Obsession — made for $750,000 by a digital creator and grossing close to $430M worldwide via Focus Features — as "undisputed economic evidence" that the majors no longer control blockbuster supply. Counsel for the states answered that breakouts do not define a market: "I'm not saying no one can have a super hit or a breakout, but there are five majors that make blockbusters consistently."

Paramount also pointed to streamers entering theatrical, citing F1 as an Amazon success before correcting that it was an Apple film. The states' retort: Apple made "a successful big movie, but it was distributed by Warner Bros. Apple makes cell phones, not movies."

Divergence flagged: earlier reporting named a different district judge as assigned to the emergency motion; today's Deadline and THR accounts both place Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín on the bench for Friday's hearing. This file records Martínez-Olguín per the two same-day accounts, with the earlier attribution unreconciled.

For director-driven event titles without franchise IP, the exit-poll data attributing attendance primarily to the director supports negotiating IMAX and premium-large-format screen commitments as a release condition rather than an allocation decided after opening results are known.

Netflix Brings Back Free Trials, Pulls Back On Viewership Data, And Starts Behaving Like A Challenger Again
Netflix's granular viewership reporting only began in December 2023, and France's TF1 channels are now being bundled into the service with more partnerships signalled.
CEO Summary
Netflix is reintroducing free trials in some markets, a practice abandoned in 2020, while cutting show-level viewership reporting from twice a year to once annually. Active experiments include YouTube-style shows, video podcasts, live channels and cloud games, and France's TF1 channels are being bundled into the service with more partnerships signalled.
Why This Matters
Sarandos's stated method, expanding gradually and moving only where the company believes it has "the right to win," frames the experiment slate as a set of options rather than commitments. Presence in a new vertical is therefore not evidence of durable spending there. An early-stage deal in any of the named experiment areas is a test the company has effectively pre-announced its willingness to abandon before investing at material scale.
Specific Implication
An agreement with a Netflix viewership-based bonus, renewal, or performance trigger should specify a defined reporting metric, audit right, and disclosure schedule in the contract rather than relying on Netflix's voluntary reporting. That reporting has moved from twice-yearly to annual. Separately, TF1's channels being added to the service through a bundling arrangement is described by Netflix as a distribution partnership rather than a content commission. That distinction is relevant to how comparable arrangements are classified in future deals.
The Facts
Free trialsNetflix is reintroducing free trials in some markets, a practice it abandoned in 2020; not currently available in the U.S. (first reported by What's On Netflix)

Sarandos on method"When we expand into new entertainment offerings, new initiatives, we do it gradually. Peters on partnerships"Whether through licensing or through new partnerships like TF1, we believe that we can help other producers, other services maximize the value, the relevance of the content that they invest in by finding those bigger audiences."

Paramount-WBD: Emergency Motions, A Showdown Hearing And Next Steps
The states' theory is modeled on DOJ's Penguin Random House win over author pay; Paramount counters with AT&T-Time Warner, a case the government lost that was unwound three years later.
CEO Summary
Twelve state AGs led by California's Rob Bonta filed for a TRO and preliminary injunction against Paramount's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, with Judge P. Casey Pitts asked to rule before July 22 and a hearing set for Friday. The states' theory rests on a narrow "anticipated top-grossing films" submarket, modeled on DOJ's successful Penguin Random House challenge. The WGA filed a separate labor-market suit the same day.
Why This Matters
The precedent choice defines the case. By importing the Penguin Random House framework, where the injury was to what authors were paid, the states have filed what is functionally a creator-compensation case wearing a distribution-share complaint. If that framing survives the emergency stage, studio consolidation gets measured in court against what sellers of films and labor are paid, a theory with reach well beyond this merger.
Specific Implication
The merger's outcome will not be resolved by the July 22 emergency ruling or the Friday hearing, and the litigation could extend well past that date. Deals under negotiation with either company should therefore carry a change-of-control clause rather than assume the current corporate structure holds for the length of a long-term commitment.

Paramount-WBD: Emergency Motions, A Showdown Hearing And Next Steps In Challenge To Mega-Merger
Paramount's counsel, Jeff Kessler, told CNBC the company would take the case up to the Supreme Court if it had to; the DOJ closed its own investigation in June with no objection.
CEO Summary
California AG Rob Bonta and 11 other state AGs filed for a TRO and preliminary injunction to halt Paramount's roughly $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, with a hearing set for Friday and a ruling requested before July 22. The states allege the combined company would hold about 30% of the "anticipated top-grossing" theatrical market and, together with Disney, 59% of top-grossing film distribution. The DOJ already closed its own investigation in June with no objection.
Why This Matters
The complaint's leverage lives in its market definitions rather than its concentration math. The alleged theatrical share moves from about 27% to about 30% depending on whether the screen threshold is 600 or 3,000 theatres. A challenge whose headline number shifts with the screen-count cutoff invites the court to dispose of the case on definitional grounds without ever reaching the merits of consolidation. Friday's hearing is therefore less a referendum on the merger than on whether the states' narrowest market survives first contact.
Specific Implication
Any deal or negotiation premised on Warner Bros. Discovery's status as an independent company, or on Paramount's post-merger scale, should treat that status as unresolved until the July 22 ruling.

That converts an advocacy point into an output floor the combined studio would have to live with.

CEO Summary

The shareholder letter's pivot to "quality and variety" retires the one engagement measure outsiders could audit without naming a successor, leaving the company as sole arbiter of whether a title performed. Any deal term keyed to Netflix engagement or viewership performance should specify the exact metric and its definition in writing. The company has stated that hours watched no longer fully determines how it evaluates a title's performance.

Netflix Content Spend Rises To ~$20B As Sarandos Says Gen AI Has Been Used On 300 Titles
The cited example is 17 minutes of AI-enhanced footage in a documentary, produced twice as fast at half the cost; live programming will be about 5 percent of total spend.
CEO Summary
Netflix will spend about $20B on content in 2026, up roughly 10%, and Ted Sarandos said generative AI workflows have been used on about 300 titles, concentrated in post-production. He cited a documentary sequence produced twice as fast at half the cost and said the savings are reinvested into more content.
Why This Matters
Every disclosed use sits on the post-production side of the line that guild AI provisions police most closely, principal photography and performance. Sarandos's remark that these use cases "are scaling faster and faster" is the operative signal. Post-production is where AI savings compound without triggering the consent and notice obligations that attach once the tools touch cast or set. Adoption will therefore grow fastest exactly where contractual visibility is weakest.
Specific Implication
Any budget or savings figure referencing "twice as fast, at half the cost" should be checked against the underlying production type. Netflix's cited example was a documentary post-production sequence rather than a scripted production with cast and crew.

Asked directly about Lionsgate and NBCUniversal, Netflix's co-CEOs said the company remains "primarily builders, not buyers" with a "very high bar" for big M&A, the same language it used before bidding for WBD. Peters said there are no near-term plans for a free ad-supported tier, and the TF1 live-broadcast partnership in France was framed as a model the company would repeat.

Netflix's characterization of the TF1 arrangement as a distribution partnership rather than an acquisition points to a deal shape: distributing existing IP through Netflix's reach without a sale. A rights holder wary of an outright sale could raise that as a comparable structure.

Promise AI, an LA startup backed by North Road, Google and a16z, has paired credited working professionals, including a Doctor Who director and the writer who developed Sharknado, with AI filmmakers on named projects, with one animated short series already in production. All financing so far comes from Promise; mainstream distribution remains unsecured.
Why This Matters
The threshold crossed is reputational rather than technical: credited professionals paid to attach their names are what erode a norm the trade itself describes as historically taboo. That weakens the collective posture guild negotiators depend on before any contract language changes.
Specific Implication
Promise AI's Pixar comparison, iterating development drafts faster and cheaper, locates the emerging AI cost pressure at the development and rewrite stage rather than on-set production.

The Video Game IP Boom Is About to Hit the Wall
Borderlands cost more than $110 million and returned just $33 million globally, and Xbox laid off 3,200 workers, a fifth of its staff, after its spending strategy misfired.
CEO Summary
More than half of the 50 best-selling game franchises of all time are already adapted or in development, and the dominant younger-audience titles, Fortnite, Minecraft and Roblox at roughly 40% of playtime, have almost no story to adapt. Gaming's own economics, 7-to-10-year builds, $1B+ budgets and mass layoffs, are not generating replacement franchises.
Why This Matters
The remaining pool is thinner than the halfway count implies: of the unadapted top-50 franchises, three originated in other media and six are sports games, leaving little that is both narrative and available. With supply compressed that far while buyers from Netflix to A24 to Paramount stay active in the category, the predictable failure mode is late-cycle pricing on mid-tier titles that lack the built-in audiences the early adaptations traded on. That is where the next Borderlands-scale loss gets made.
Specific Implication
Rights holders of the remaining unadapted narrative game franchises are negotiating scarce supply against buyers still active in the category. The Borderlands loss is the comp buyers will cite to hold price on mid-tier titles.

WGA Joins The Fight, Federal Judge Sets Friday Hearing: Paramount-WBD Merger Heads For A Pre-July-22 Showdown

CEO Summary
The Writers Guild of America sued Tuesday in the Northern District of California to block Paramount Skydance's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on a labor-monopsony theory, one day after 12 state AGs filed their antitrust suit. Judge P. Casey Pitts hears the states' emergency TRO motion Friday July 17 and is asked to rule before July 22, the window in which Paramount could otherwise close. Paramount responded with a public commitment to at least 30 movies a year with full 45-day theatrical windows.
Why This Matters
The number that travels beyond this deal sits in the Facts: under the states' "anticipated top-grossing" submarket definition, Paramount-WBD plus Disney would together control 59% of tentpole distribution. If Judge Pitts accepts that submarket as legally cognizable, the precedent constrains every future studio combination and puts Disney's own share within reach of the same theory. That gives the majors a structural reason to prefer this case settled rather than decided.
Specific Implication
Talent and representatives with active or pending deals at Paramount or Warner Bros. Discovery are negotiating with two companies that still compete with each other for material and talent. That dynamic changes once the merger closes.
The Facts
  • The Writers Guild of America (East + West jointly) sued in the Northern District of California on Tuesday July 14 to block Paramount Skydance's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, one day after 12 state AGs filed their own antitrust suit. The WGA complaint is a labor-market (monopsony) theory: fewer competitors would let the merged entity "lower costs by suppressing writers' wages and reducing output."
  • The state AGs' emergency-relief motion (TRO + preliminary injunction) was assigned to U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts, with a hearing set for Friday July 17 and a ruling asked for before July 22 — the window in which Paramount could otherwise close (the EU is also expected to rule around July 22).
  • The states allege three harmed markets: wide-release theatrical (combined ~27% share at the 600+ theater threshold), "anticipated top-grossing" blockbusters (~30% at the 3,000+ theater threshold; Paramount-WBD + Disney together = 59% of that submarket), and basic cable channel licensing (27% by affiliate fees, 34% by viewership).
  • Paramount's response: it will commit to "at least 30 movies a year, with full 45-day windows," continue commissioning from independent producers, maintain two distinct film studios under independent creative leadership, and argues its true competitive market includes Amazon, Apple and Netflix.
  • Legal teams: Paramount has retained Paul Clement and Jeff Kessler (alongside Daniel Petrocelli, who beat DOJ's AT&T–Time Warner challenge in 2018, and Makan Delrahim, that case's DOJ antitrust chief, now Paramount's CLO).
  • Antitrust read (William Kovacic, ex-FTC chair, GW Law): the states' complaint is "good enough to give Paramount and Warner Brothers a hard time"; the likely endgame is a settlement converting executives' verbal promises into a binding order plus concessions to protect the theatrical channel and possibly a no-workforce-reduction funding commitment (the merger targets $6B in cost savings).

Paramount–WBD Fight Escalates: Ellisons Sued Over Alleged Trump 'Side Deal,' Antitrust Hearing Friday, AG Nominee Grilled

CEO Summary
A Paramount shareholder sued David and Larry Ellison in Delaware Chancery Court to block the $111B WBD merger, alleging they promised private benefits to President Trump to clear regulatory barriers; Paramount denies any commitments were made. The suit landed a day after the state AGs' antitrust action and the WGA's labor suit, with Judge Pitts set to hear the emergency injunction motion Friday and rule before July 22. At his Senate confirmation hearing, AG nominee Todd Blanche confirmed he was part of the DOJ's June sign-off decision.
Why This Matters
The Blanche testimony is the piece with legal consequence. His acknowledgment that he was part of the June sign-off pairs with the WSJ report that senior leadership closed the probe before career staff who leaned toward a challenge could object. Together they degrade the DOJ clearance's persuasive value before Judge Pitts. A clearance that looks politically administered stops functioning as evidence the deal is lawful, which leaves Paramount defending the merger on the merits as if no federal review had blessed it.
The Facts
  • A Paramount shareholder (lead plaintiff Paul Robbins, repped by Thomas Law/Public Integrity Project/Freedom of the Press Foundation) sued David and Larry Ellison in Delaware Chancery Court on Tuesday, seeking to block the $111B WBD merger and unspecified damages. The suit alleges the Ellisons promised "illegal private benefits to President Trump to remove federal regulatory barriers" — including settling Trump's CNN legal claims to "funnel cash" to him and firing CNN anchors Trump dislikes after the takeover. Trump is not named as a defendant.
  • Paramount's response: the suit "recycles allegations already reported and already addressed," and "no commitments from either David or Larry Ellison have been made to any government body… regarding the future of CNN or any other news property." It reiterated the deal "stands on its own merits."
  • The complaint landed a day after 12 Democratic state AGs (led by California's Rob Bonta) filed a federal antitrust suit; the WGA also sued on labor grounds. The AG case was assigned to U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts, who must rule on the states' emergency TRO/preliminary-injunction motion before July 22; a hearing is set for Friday (July 17). A granted TRO would freeze the deal for weeks. (Deadline also reported Paramount sought recusal of an initially-assigned judge, hence the reassignment.)
  • The states' market-share case: the combined entity would hold ~27% of wide-release theatrical (600+ theater threshold) and ~30% of top-grossing theatrical (3,000+ threshold); Paramount-WBD + Disney together would control 59% of the top-grossing market; ~27–34% of basic cable. Antitrust experts (William Kovacic, ex-FTC chair) call the complaint strong enough to force a serious fight and predict a settlement with binding commitments over the spoken CNN/journalism promises, possibly workforce guarantees (vs. the merger's $6B cost-savings target). Paramount's team: Paul Clement and Jeff Kessler.
  • At his Senate confirmation hearing Wednesday, AG nominee Todd Blanche (Trump's former personal lawyer, acting AG) told Sen. Cory Booker "I was part of that decision" on the DOJ's June 12 sign-off but claimed "no idea" whether career Antitrust Division staff recommended closing the probe. The WSJ reported senior leadership closed the investigation before career staffers — who leaned toward challenging the deal — could object. Booker also pressed Blanche on attending an April Paramount dinner honoring Trump while the DOJ probe was open.
  • Separately, the suit flags no visible CFIUS review despite $24B from Saudi, Qatari and UAE sovereign funds that would own 38.5% of the combined company (Paramount says no board seats/voting shares, so no CFIUS trigger).

FCC Sets Aug. 6 Vote to Repeal the National Broadcast Ownership Cap
Nexstar, blocked by a federal court from buying Tegna under the current cap, backs the repeal; Commissioner Anna Gomez calls it unlawful and says only Congress can change it.
CEO Summary
The FCC signaled it will vote August 6 to repeal the cap barring a single owner from controlling TV stations reaching more than 39% of U.S. markets, replacing it with case-by-case transaction review. Nexstar, blocked by a federal court from acquiring Tegna under the cap, backs the repeal; Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez calls it unlawful, arguing only Congress can change a statutory cap.
Why This Matters
Replacing a bright-line cap with case-by-case review moves the constraint from rule to regulator. Transaction approval becomes discretionary. In a commission whose chairman argued the case in a Breitbart op-ed, that discretion converts station M&A into a political-alignment exercise, favoring buyers with administration relationships over buyers with the strongest balance sheets.
The Facts
  • The FCC signaled it will vote Aug. 6 to repeal the longstanding cap that bars a single owner from controlling TV stations reaching more than 39% of U.S. markets, replacing it with a case-by-case review of individual transactions.
  • Chairman Brendan Carr (op-ed in Breitbart) argued the cap is obsolete because national programmers already reach 100% of the country via their own streaming services and virtual MVPDs like YouTube TV, and cable/social/Netflix face no equivalent limit.
  • Immediate consequence: Nexstar — a top station owner (also owns the CW network and NewsNation) — has been blocked by a federal court from completing its acquisition of Tegna on grounds it would give Nexstar too much local-TV control. Nexstar backs the repeal.
  • Dissent + legal risk: Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez called it "unlawful," arguing Congress set the 39% cap in federal law and "only Congress" can raise or eliminate it — signaling likely litigation. The NAB (broadcaster trade group) applauded the move.
  • The FCC stressed repeal is not automatic deal approval: transactions exceeding the old 39% cap could still be denied if not in the public interest, or approved if they are.

Discovery, then filed the same evening for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction in San Francisco federal court, warning the deal could close as soon as July 22. Why This Matters
The $7M per day ticking fee that begins September 30, 2026 converts litigation delay itself into leverage for the states. Overall or first-look deals tied to WBD face renewal terms that could shift once a combined Paramount-WBD entity begins consolidating redundant agreements, a risk that exists only if the merger closes.
The Facts

Discovery, then filed a motion the same evening for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction in federal court in San Francisco, warning Paramount could otherwise close as soon as July 22.
  • The suit alleges the merger violates the Clayton Act by concentrating three markets: wide-release theatrical distribution, "anticipated top-grossing"/tentpole theatrical distribution (a market Bonta argues is legally distinct), and basic cable channel licensing — giving the combined company 27% of wide-release distribution, 30% of the tentpole submarket, and 27% of the basic-cable bundle.
  • The merger agreement's outside date is March 4, 2027 (auto-extending to June 4, 2027 if antitrust review is pending), with a $7M/day ticking fee on Paramount starting September 30, 2026.
  • The DOJ already cleared the deal in March 2026; the EU is expected to rule around the same July 22 window. The UK's competition watchdog has also opened a formal investigation.

The IFPI and RIAA framing of the labels as "an immediately understandable and easily scalable approach to transparency" fixes the industry's posture as disclosure rather than restriction. The Facts
  • A coalition — RIAA, IFPI, the Grammys, SAG-AFTRA, the Human Artistry Campaign (plus A2IM, WIN, IMPALA) — introduced two voluntary labels for sound recordings: "AI-Generated" (AI used for the entirety or primary portion) and "AI-Assisted" (substantially human, AI for some expressive elements).
  • The icons are designed for adoption by digital music services and distributors. They do not yet cover AI use in lyrics, composition, music videos, or cover art.
  • The eye-opening data: Deezer reported 44% of all new music on its platform is AI-generated; Apple Music reported more than one-third of its tracks are "100% AI."
  • IFPI/RIAA leadership: "Fans want to know whether and how generative AI has been used… these labels will provide an immediately understandable and easily scalable approach to transparency."

The Get-Big-or-Die Era of European TV: Sky Buys ITV for $2.1B
Sky's £1.6B ITV deal excludes ITV Studios, which spins off separately with a Sky programming commitment of at least £2.1B for 2028-2032; two days later the BBC confirmed its own Channel 4 streaming talks.
CEO Summary
Comcast-owned Sky agreed to acquire ITV's broadcasting and streaming operations for £1.6B ($2.1B), combining Britain's largest pay-TV operator with its largest commercial free-to-air broadcaster; ITV Studios spins off as a standalone listed content business with a ≥£2.1B Sky programming commitment for 2028-2032. Two days later the BBC confirmed talks with Channel 4 about a combined streaming platform, and parallel consolidation is moving in Germany, Italy, and Spain.
Why This Matters
Regulators cleared the Sky-ITV combination, RTL's acquisition of Sky Deutschland, and MediaForEurope's cross-border stake-building in Spain, Italy and Portugal within a compressed period. The BBC confirmed talks with Channel 4 on a combined streaming platform two days after the Sky-ITV announcement. The pattern spans multiple national markets and ownership groups rather than a single deal.

A separate model has emerged in France. TF1 and, separately, France Télévisions and M6 signed carriage deals placing their channels and on-demand content inside Netflix's and Amazon's interfaces rather than merging with another broadcaster. RTVE signed a comparable deal with Amazon in Spain. Both the consolidation path and the carriage-deal path reduce the number of independently owned broadcasters operating without a merger partner or platform agreement.
Specific Implication
Anyone selling rights or formats into these markets now negotiates against fewer independently owned counterparties.
The Facts
  • Comcast-owned Sky agreed to acquire ITV's broadcasting and streaming operations for £1.6B ($2.1B) — combining Britain's largest pay-TV operator with its largest commercial free-to-air broadcaster. The deal excludes ITV Studios (Coronation Street, Love Island), which spins off as a standalone London-listed content business; Sky committed to ≥£2.1B ($2.8B) in ITV Studios programming spend for 2028–2032.
  • Two days later, the BBC said it is in talks with Channel 4 to combine streaming into a single British "sovereign platform."
  • The wave is Europe-wide: Germany's RTL cleared to buy Comcast's Sky Deutschland; the Berlusconi-family MediaForEurope controls ProSiebenSat.1 plus assets in Spain/Italy/Portugal.
  • The alternative model (France): rather than merge, TF1 struck a carriage deal to distribute through Netflix; France Télévisions and M6 signed similar deals with Amazon Prime Video, and Amazon added RTVE in Spain. Regulators who blocked such tie-ups for two decades are now clearing them, deciding global streamers/ad giants — not domestic TV consolidation — are the primary competitive threat.

Even combined, Sky and ITV's 17.7 percent viewing share still trails YouTube's 18.6 percent, and the agreement keeps ITV Studios' flagship series free-to-air rather than moving them behind Sky's paywall. That structure shows what the acquisition is actually buying: advertising reach at national scale, not subscription exclusivity. It marks a shift in legacy-TV consolidation logic from paywall conversion toward defensive audience aggregation against the platforms.
Specific Implication
A production arm structured as a formally separate entity from an acquired network can have its supply agreement preserved and extended through the acquisition, as ITV Studios' £2.1B output deal shows.
The Facts
  • Comcast/NBCUniversal-owned Sky has agreed to acquire ITV's television network and streaming (ITVX) operations for £1.6B ($2.1B). ITV confirmed to shareholders Monday morning. Structure: £1.2B upfront + £200M payable H1 2028, contingent on ITV ad revenue hitting £1.7B next year; ~£950M cash return (25p/share) to ITV shareholders.
  • ITV Studios (the production arm — Love Island, Coronation Street, I'm a Celebrity) is NOT part of the deal and stays independent. Sky struck a separate £2.1B output deal with ITV Studios through 2032 to keep producing those series (they will not move behind Sky's paywall), and is selling Bake Off producer Love Productions to ITV Studios in a £200M side-deal.
  • Combined Sky+ITV TV/streaming viewing share was 17.7% in May, just behind YouTube's 18.6% (Barb). ITV generated £2B revenue in 2025, ~32% commercial-viewing share; ITVX has ~16.5M monthly active users.
  • Sits under NBCUniversal, which Comcast is spinning out as a standalone listed company. Nearly nine-month courtship since ITV's November notice. Follows the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger moving toward completion.

Behind The 'Supergirl' Bomb: Competing Cuts, Creative Differences

Discovery; a formal notice would trigger 40-day Ofcom and CMA reviews, and a phase-two referral could push closing into early 2027. A Major Theater Chain Forward-Integrates Into Distribution to Fill the Festival-to-Theatrical Gap
Alamo Exclusives launches with a SXSW music documentary, tickets on sale July 21, and plans to pull further titles from Sundance, Tribeca, TIFF, Cannes, Berlin and its own Fantastic Fest.
CEO Summary
Alamo Drafthouse is launching Alamo Exclusives, a distribution label giving unreleased festival titles limited theatrical runs on its own screens. It debuts with a SXSW music documentary and plans programming from Sundance, SXSW, Tribeca, TIFF, Cannes, Berlin and Fantastic Fest, working directly with filmmakers on presentation and marketing.
Why This Matters
An exhibitor stepping into the distributor's slot changes who prices the failure of the acquisition market. Limited runs confined to one chain's own screens provide exposure without a nationwide footprint or a standard P&A commitment. The label therefore functions less as a rival to a conventional distribution deal than as a floor beneath it. The existence of that floor marginally weakens a distributor's ability to present any theatrical release at all as a concession in negotiation.
Specific Implication
A festival film that fails to secure standard distribution now has a direct-to-venue theatrical option through this label.
The Facts
Alamo Drafthouse is launching a distribution label, Alamo Exclusives, offering limited-run theatrical engagements on its own screens to unreleased festival titles. The chain frames it as a response to the growing difficulty independently financed festival films face in finding nationwide theatrical distribution. It launches with a SXSW music documentary (tickets July 21) and plans future programming from Sundance, SXSW, Tribeca, TIFF, Cannes, Berlin, and its own Fantastic Fest. The chain works directly with filmmakers, providing presentation, marketing, and theatrical exposure.

Sony PlayStation to End Physical Game Disc Production by 2028 — Another Ownership-to-Access Domino Falls
US game consumer spend grew just 1 percent to $60.7 billion in 2025 while subscription revenue rose 20 percent, the math Sony cited for retiring the format it launched in 1994.
CEO Summary
Sony Interactive Entertainment will end production of new PlayStation game discs by January 2028, citing consumer preference for digital. The move routes every new game sale through the PlayStation Store; US game subscription revenue grew 20% in 2025 while total spend was roughly flat at $60.7B.
Why This Matters
The stated rationale, a "general preference for digital media," names the demand side and omits the supply-side prize. Retiring the disc eliminates used-game resale and the retail intermediary in one move, leaving every transaction inside a storefront where the platform holder sets the price and takes the margin. The format decision is best read as a move to full channel control that consumer preference makes politically costless.

Getty Images Abandons $3.7 Billion Merger With Shutterstock
Why This Matters
The Getty-Shutterstock merger received unconditional US Department of Justice antitrust clearance in February 2026, but Getty's board terminated the deal after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority conditioned approval on a divestiture Getty's board deemed a non-starter. US antitrust clearance did not extend to UK regulatory approval on this transaction.
Specific Implication
A transaction that clears US antitrust review does not thereby clear UK Competition and Markets Authority review; a merger under active review in both jurisdictions carries the UK outcome as a separate, non-derivative risk.
The Facts
Getty Images's board unanimously terminated its proposed $3.7B merger with Shutterstock after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) conditioned approval on Shutterstock divesting its editorial/celebrity/news photo business (Backgrid, Splash News, and related units) — a requirement Getty's board deemed a non-starter. The US Department of Justice had already granted unconditional antitrust clearance in February 2026. Shutterstock shares fell roughly 29-30% on the news. Getty faces a breakup fee and note-redemption obligations, and its board is now hiring a financial advisor to assess "strategic financing alternatives." Days before terminating the deal, Getty separately signed a licensing agreement with OpenAI for its image library across ChatGPT.

YouTube and Meta Now Out-Earn the Studios, and They Are Coming for the TV Screen
YouTube passed $60 billion in revenue and Meta's Reels makes over $50 billion a year, more than Paramount, WBD and NBCUniversal combined, while legacy media answers with Fox-Roku and the $111 billion Paramount-WBD deal, per THR.
The Hollywood Reporter frames the next few years as a zero-sum fight for the TV screen. YouTube is now the world's largest media company at more than $60 billion in revenue and dominates TV watch time. Meta says Reels makes more than $50 billion a year, more than Paramount Skydance, WBD and NBCUniversal combined, and Instagram is testing longform episodes with a Samsung deal to bake the app into TVs. Legacy media's answer is scale: Fox's $22 billion Roku deal and the $111 billion Paramount-WBD combination. The same month Amazon dropped Guadagnino's Artificial and Apple parted with Jon Stewart.
Potential Talent Implication: Tech platforms have the money and the audience but the worst record on creative control, so talent weighing a tech-platform deal on sensitive material may need abandonment, reversion and release commitments that a studio deal would not require.
The Facts
A connect-the-dots analysis arguing the next few years are a zero-sum fight between legacy Hollywood and Big Tech for the TV screen and total attention:
  • YouTube is now the world's largest media company (>$60B revenue last year) and dominates TV watch time (Nielsen Gauge), while most other streamers are flat/down and Netflix stagnates.
  • Meta says Reels (Instagram + Facebook) generates >$50B/yr in ad revenue: more than Paramount Skydance, WBD and NBCUniversal combined: and is now pushing onto TV (Instagram testing episodic longform horizontal video; a Samsung deal bakes the app into all its TVs).
  • Legacy's counter is scale via megadeals: Fox's $22B deal for Roku (platform leverage for the streaming era) and David Ellison's $111B Paramount Skydance + WBD combine (financed in part by Oracle, with Larry Ellison pledging Oracle shares as a backstop). Netflix is also reported to be eyeing deals.
  • Big Tech's creative-stewardship record is mixed: **Amazon MGM dropped Luca Guadagnino's OpenAI/Sam Altman film Artificial mid-production (Netflix, A24, Focus also passed); Amazon recently signed a multibillion-dollar OpenAI deal. The same day, A24 announced a $75M AI deal with Google. Apple** dropped a Gawker project and parted ways with Jon Stewart over content differences.

The Hollywood Reporter profiles writers, editors, storyboard artists and a former HBO development executive moonlighting on reinforcement learning from human feedback, training the systems many fear will replace them.   • As the traditional film/TV job market narrows, creatives (writers, editors, development execs, storyboard artists) are moonlighting in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF): training the gen-AI systems many fear will displace them. Amazon MGM Is Open for Business Again Under Peter Friedlander

Peter Friedlander, eight months into running Amazon MGM Studios' TV side after Jen Salke, has scrapped the wholly-owned versus co-production split for a drama and comedy, world-building, animation and non-scripted structure, with Blair Fetter on genre and Jenn Levy on non-scripted. The Facts

Netflix Subscribers Are Watching Less
Netflix hours viewed rose 2 percent in the second half of 2025 while subscribers grew about 10 percent, daily minutes per user fell from 100.5 to 93.4, and YouTube passed it on time spent, per Puck.
Puck reports Netflix stock is down about a third since it moved to bid for Warner Bros. in November, and the growth story has softened underneath. Total hours viewed rose 2 percent in the second half of 2025 while subscribers grew roughly 10 percent, an 8 percent drop in engagement per subscriber. Daily minutes per user fell from 100.5 to 93.4 while YouTube rose to 99.1 and became the fastest-growing platform by time spent. The second half of 2026 has fewer marquee titles and no video podcast has charted on Nielsen's top 10.
Potential Talent Implication: A buyer with a thin marquee pipeline and pressure to show a hit may pay up for talent that reliably draws attention, so proven creators could have more leverage on guarantees at Netflix right now even as new mega-deals get harder.
The Facts
  • Netflix stock is down ~one-third from early November, when it moved to bid on Warner Bros.: and didn't recover even after losing WBD to Paramount Skydance; the M&A about-face left an "impression of weakness."
  • Roku interest was "way early"; Netflix never bid (Roku not worth near the $22B Fox paid). Rumors of Netflix pursuing Lionsgate are "B.S., at least for now."
  • Growth has slowed: H2-2025 total hours viewed +2% while global subs (MoffettNathanson est.) grew ~10% → ~8% decline in daily engagement per subscriber.
  • Daily minutes/user fell 100.5 → 93.4 (2024→2025) per Digital i; YouTube rose 87.2 → 99.1 over the same period and is now the fastest-growing platform by time spent.
  • Thin slate of breakout hits on the season's biggest-shows list (only Stranger Things: now ended: plus Bridgerton and limited series His & Hers); H2-2026 has fewer marquee titles and tough comps (last year's KPop Demon Hunters, Stranger Things, Wednesday).
  • Video-podcast push: no video podcast has charted on Nielsen's weekly top 10; internal podcast engagement reported "low."

Warner Bros. Gets Sold Either Way
With DOJ approval in hand, California's Rob Bonta is the last threat to the $110 billion Paramount-Warner deal; if it fails, Plan B is to auction the studio and HBO Max to Netflix or Comcast, per Puck.
The Justice Department approved the roughly $110 billion Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on June 12, leaving California Attorney General Rob Bonta as the remaining live threat. If California blocks the deal, Puck reports, Warner Bros. splits the studio and HBO Max from its networks and auctions them to Netflix or Comcast, collecting a breakup fee near $7 billion. Analyst Rich Greenfield's read is that the company gets sold either way. Paramount is expected to cut toward $6 billion in synergies; Quinta Brunson has already moved her overall deal from Warner Bros. TV to Disney.

The Facts
  • DOJ already approved the ~$110B Paramount Skydance–WBD deal (June 12, 2026). The remaining live threat is California AG Rob Bonta, expected to sue.
  • Belloni's scenarios if California acts: a judge enjoins the deal; the state unwinds it; or the saga drags into 2027 and the Ellisons tire of the ~$650M-per-quarter "ticking fee" and walk (he doubts the last).
  • Plan B = the split (originally Plan A): separate the Warners studio + HBO Max from the TV networks and auction them: likely buyers Netflix or Comcast, the two jilted suitors. Netflix would bid less without the Ellison/Middle East money against it; Comcast's ability is doubtful (shares near decade lows).
  • Breakup economics: Warners would likely collect a ~$7B breakup fee from Paramount (on top of the $2.8B Paramount already owes Netflix for spoiling that earlier closed deal). A spun-off "Discovery Global" would hand Gunnar Wiedenfels his own company.
  • Paramount is expected to "slash and burn" to ~$6B in synergies; Netflix as owner would likely retain more of the Warners workforce.
  • The industry "Block the Merger" campaign has passed 4,000+ signatures (incl. Denis Villeneuve, Cynthia Nixon, Javier Bardem, Nia DaCosta); Paramount has accused Netflix of a "panic-level… scorched-earth campaign to poison regulators" (June 5 letter to DOJ); Netflix denies involvement.
  • Greenfield to Belloni: "There is no scenario in which this company is an ongoing entity like it is today. It is getting sold, the only question is to whom."

Toy Story 5 Opens to a Record $160 Million
Toy Story 5 opened to $160 million domestic and $312 million worldwide, a franchise record and the best opening of 2026, with a Taylor Swift song at number one on the Hot 100 before release.
Toy Story 5 opened to $160 million domestic and $312 million worldwide, the best opening of 2026, a franchise record and the second-best animated opening ever behind Incredibles 2. It drew 11.5 million admissions, a 95 percent Rotten Tomatoes score and the franchise's fourth A CinemaScore. A Taylor Swift original song reached number one on the Hot 100 before release and 26 percent of the audience was women under 25; promotional partners contributed a record $200 million in media. Pixar originals Elio, Elemental and Hoppers opened between $21 million and $45 million.
Potential Talent Implication: Family animation is the strongest theatrical category right now, so talent attached to a franchise animated title has more leverage to insist on a theatrical commitment and sequel backend than talent attached to an original.

Lily James Leads an Amazon MGM Horror Film From 21 Laps and Atomic Monster
Lily James will star in Seasons, Drew Hancock's follow-up to Companion, for Amazon MGM, produced by 21 Laps and Blumhouse's Atomic Monster from a viral Reddit horror short.
Lily James will star in Seasons, an Amazon MGM horror feature from writer-director Drew Hancock, his follow-up to New Line's Companion. The story comes from a viral Reddit short turned novel by Matt and Harrison Query about a couple whose ranch is alive with spirits that demand seasonal rituals. Shawn Levy and Dan Levine's 21 Laps produce with Jason Blum and Michael Clear's Atomic Monster, their third collaboration, plus 12:01 Films and Dan Cohen.
Potential Talent Implication: Elevated horror built on viral IP, a star and a hot genre director now has at least three buyers paying for the same profile, which gives horror filmmakers and writers a real bidding field to price against.

Apple Says It Has No Fixed Rules on Theatrical Windows
Eddy Cue told Cannes Lions that Apple keeps films in theaters as long as tickets sell before streaming; F1 took $634 million and Cue and Jerry Bruckheimer expect a sequel.
Eddy Cue and Jerry Bruckheimer told a Cannes Lions audience they expect an F1 sequel after the first film took $634 million worldwide, Brad Pitt's biggest. Bruckheimer said he pitched nine exhibitors and studios and Apple won with the most flexible plan: a 45-day theatrical exclusive, then cinemas for as long as people bought tickets, then streaming. Cue said there are no hard and fast rules on windows and that Apple never licensed a library by design. Bruckheimer credited Cue personally with getting the film made; the two are reteaming with Joseph Kosinski on a UAP thriller.
Potential Talent Implication: Filmmakers who want a full theatrical run with a streamer's budget now have a buyer saying so on the record, which can be used as leverage when Netflix or Amazon offers a rigid window.
The Facts

WindowingBruckheimer pitched 9 exhibitors/studios; Apple won with the most "creative" plan: 45-day theatrical, then left it in cinemas "as long as people were buying tickets," then streaming
Cue doctrine"You can't have hard and fast rules" on windows (film or TV); "be flexible and move quickly… do the right thing for that particular moment"
Greenlight authorityBruckheimer: "Without [Cue]… I don't think the movie would have gotten made": Cue (an F1/sports fan) as the decider
Other Apple projectBruckheimer + Joseph Kosinski reteam on a UAP/UFO thriller ("All the President's Men about what the government has been hiding")

Paramount Locks Dan Trachtenberg Into a Three-Year First-Look and an Animated Family Film
Dan Trachtenberg signed a three-year first-look deal with Paramount and will direct the animated PG comedy Freddy the 13th under new Paramount Animation president Jennifer Dodge.
Paramount announced Freddy the 13th at Annecy, an animated PG family comedy from a graphic novel, directed by Dan Trachtenberg with the book's author Yehudi Mercado. Warner Bros. Hands a Feature to the Creator of Hazbin Hotel
Warner Bros. Pictures Animation set Prehistoria, the feature directing debut of YouTube-native creator Vivienne Medrano, and dated Bad Fairies with Cynthia Erivo and Ncuti Gatwa for May 21, 2027.
Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, under president Bill Damaschke, announced Prehistoria, an original animated musical and the feature directing debut of Vivienne Medrano, the YouTube-native creator of Hazbin Hotel and Helluva Boss with billions of views.
